pool.q: An 80-year-old woman reports persistent flashes OU with worsening night vision over 2 months. She has constricted visual fields by confrontation and bilateral retinal pigment deposition anterior to the arcade vessels. Full-field electroretinogram (ERG) shows minimal signal from both eyes. What is the suggested management for this patient?

options.a: audiometry and fitting for hearing aids if needed
options.b: genetic testing and examination of family members for similar findings
options.c: serum testing and evaluation of chest/abdomen/pelvis for mass lesions
options.d: genetic testing and urgent cardiology consultation for electrocardiogram

pool.rationale:
Paraneoplastic syndromes such as cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) present with constant photopsias, impaired color vision, nyctalopia, impaired dark adaptation, dimming, ring scotoma, and peripheral and/or central visual field loss. The fundus can initially appear normal, but the ERG response shows markedly reduced amplitudes. As the disease progresses, the retinal arterioles become attenuated, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) thinned and mottled, and the optic discs pale. This patient has the typical features of CAR and should undergo workup for anti-retinal antibodies and to identify an occult malignancy.
The differential diagnosis of this presentation includes other bilateral retinopathies with ERG abnormalities, including retinitis pigmentosa and its various syndromes, or mitochondrial myopathies such as Kearns-Sayre syndrome. Rod or rod-cone retinal dystrophies show similar abnormalities on ERG and can be associated with retinal pigmentation. Examination of family members is useful in determining the inheritance pattern. Pigmentary retinopathies such as Usher syndrome can be associated with hearing difficulties and require audiology consultation. Kearns-Sayre syndrome is associated with cardiac conduction blocks, a life-threatening complication, hence the need for cardiology consultation. These patients tend to present earlier in life than the patient in this case, and likely will have other retinal or ocular examination features to suggest the alternative diagnosis, for example, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia with motility dysfunction and progressive ptosis in Kearns-Sayre syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For an optic nerve glioma, what is the most likely finding on orbital imaging?

options.a: enhancement of the optic nerve sheath ("tram-tracking")
options.c: hyperintensity on T-1 weighted, precontrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
options.d: fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve

pool.rationale:
Most optic nerve gliomas (ONGs) exhibit a fusiform shape on computed tomography (CT) and MRI. Globular or multilobulated shapes may occur, but are less common. The optic nerve may also have a characteristic tortuosity or kinking. If mucinous degeneration has occurred, cystic spaces within the lesion may be evident. ONG is typically either isointense or hypointense to gray matter on precontrast T1-weighted MRI. Enhancement with gadolinium is the rule, although it is less intense than that seen in optic nerve sheath meningioma (ONSM).
"Tram-tracking" is a classic sign of ONSM, due to tumor growth along the nerve sheath. Of note, fusiform shapes are also quite common with ONSM; the optic nerve should appear as a lucency on imaging of ONSM, as opposed to ONG.
A dilated superior ophthalmic vein is usually a sign of orbital and cavernous sinus congestion and is classically seen in carotid-cavernous fistula.

pool.q: To what area of the brain does a lesion cause the combination of symptoms of formed hallucinations, insomnia, and excessive daytime somnolence?
pool.rationale: In rare cases, lesions involving the mesencephalon (midbrain) cause formed, often constant hallucinations frequently associated with an inverted sleep-wake cycle (peduncular hallucinosis). Depending on the extent of the midbrain lesion, there can be accompanying neurologic symptoms. Disorders of the nondominant parieto-occipital area cause palinopsia, the illusion of persistent afterimages that can be associated with visual hallucinations. Temporal lobe lesions most often produce olfactory and gustatory hallucinations; visual phenomena from this area are usually complex, formed hallucinations in the ipsilateral or contralateral visual field. Occipital lobe lesions commonly cause unformed hallucinations, which are sometimes described as geometric colors or patterns.

pool.q: A patient presents with signs and symptoms consistent with a compressive lesion of CNIII. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is obtained and read as negative. What would be the best next step to take?

options.a: Call neuroradiologist for review of MRI.

pool.rationale:
If a neuroimaging study does not reveal a structural lesion in the area that is suspected based on clinical examination, the physician should first review the study with a neuroradiologist to ensure that the appropriate imaging study was performed, and the area of concern was adequately imaged. Additional clinical history can be helpful to the neuroradiologist to ensure that a structural lesion was not overlooked on the original study. If the study is truly negative after review, additional workup or referral to a neuro-ophthalmologist would be appropriate.
Repeating neuroimaging would not necessarily yield the appropriate concerns. The answer choice "repeating neuroimaging" suggests that another MRI (not MRA) of the brain should be performed without first consulting the neuroradiologist and reviewing the images with them. This would not increase the likelihood of detection of an aneurysm, whereas consultation with a neuroradiologist may result in discovering a subtle lesion (as most larger aneurysms are detectable by MRI as well), and if this did not work, would lead to suggestion of cerebrovascular imaging. While in clinical practice, it is unlikely that a CN III palsy would undergo neuroimaging without cerebrovascular imaging, the most correct answer is still to ask for the neuroradiologist to review the MRI.

pool.q: A 79-year-old woman presents with an acute onset of binocular horizontal diplopia and dizziness. Examination reveals a right head turn with an esotropia that is worse on right gaze. There is decreased corneal sensation and lagophthalmos on the right. What is the location of the lesion?
pool.rationale:
This scenario describes right V (decreased corneal sensation), VI (esotropia worse on right gaze), VII (lagophthalmos), and possibly VIII cranial nerve palsies (dizziness) in combination. CPA tumors, especially acoustic neuroma or meningioma, can cause V, VI, VII, and/or VIII nerve palsies with the above findings, as well as ipsilateral decreased hearing. Other common locations of multiple cranial nerve palsies are the orbital apex, cavernous sinus, and brainstem. However, isolated orbital apex lesions do not cause decreased V, VII, or VIII nerve palsy. Cavernous sinus lesions do not affect the VII or VIII nerve. Midbrain lesions develop more rostrally than the nuclei of the described cranial nerves, and thus affect III and/or IV cranial nerves instead.

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: While hospitalized for a presumed exacerbation of asthma, a 50-year-old man is noted to have moderate right upper eyelid ptosis. The ptosis has been intermittently present for several months. The ophthalmologist discusses management of the patient with the gastroenterologist, who was called to evaluate dysphagia. What diagnostic test offers the advantages of safety, speed, and specificity?
pool.rationale: Considering the constellation of ptosis, breathing difficulties, and trouble swallowing, myasthenia gravis is a reasonable and somewhat urgent concern. After 2 minutes of cooling with an ice pack, improvement of ptosis can be seen in most patients with MG. If further testing is needed, the patient could undergo edrophonium (Tensilon) testing to confirm the diagnosis. Edrophonium testing may be associated with rare but serious adverse effects such as bradycardia, bronchospasm, cholinergic crisis, respiratory arrest, or syncopal episodes. Although antibody testing is useful, it will take time to get the results. Pupillary abnormalities are not associated with myasthenia gravis.

pool.q: For 2 months, a 67-year-old Filipino man has had blurred vision. He is on treatment for a chronic pulmonary infection from mycobacterium avium-intracellulare. His visual acuity is 20/200 OU, his color vision is reduced on D15 testing, and his optic discs show mild pallor. What pattern of visual-field loss might be expected on perimetry?
pool.rationale: Ethambutol is a common medication used in the treatment of mycobacterium avium-intracellulare. This is one of the most common medications implicated in toxic optic neuropathy. Optic neuropathy resulting from toxic exposure is characterized by a gradual, progressive, and painless vision loss. Visual fields typically show either bilateral central or cecocentral scotomas. An arcuate scotoma is a nerve fiber bundle defect typical of glaucoma. Homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing can be seen with optic tract, optic radiation, and occipital lobe lesions. Enlarged blind spots are classically seen with papilledema.

pool.q: Computerized axial tomography (CT) is usually more helpful than magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in patients with what condition?

options.c: choroidal melanomas with suspected orbital extension

pool.rationale:
CT is superior to MRI in detecting bony deformities, especially in the orbits and sinuses. Therefore, orbital fractures are best seen on orbital CT rather than on MRI, as CT allows detailed views of fracture location in relation to soft tissue.
"Chiasmal lesion" is not correct, because axial CT often misses pituitary abnormalities. Coronal T1-weighted post-gadolinium imaging is particularly useful to evaluate proximity of the optic chiasm to a pituitary mass and to identify extension into the adjacent cavernous sinuses.
"Optic neuritis" is not correct, because demyelinating disease is poorly viewed on CT. Demyelinating lesions are well-characterized by MRI with T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images of the brain, and T1-weighted fat-suppressed images with gadolinium contrast of the orbit.
"Choroidal melanoma with orbital extension" is not correct, because it is a soft tissue lesion abutting the soft tissue globe, and MRI is superior to CT in defining soft tissue borders.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 56-year-old man presents with acute onset right-sided neck pain and right upper lid ptosis following chiropractic manipulation. The pupils were 3 mm OD and 4 mm OS. He has a severe allergy to iodinated contrast. What imaging modality should be used for this patient to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
pool.rationale: This patient is presenting with symptoms of an acute painful Horner syndrome following chiropractic manipulation, which is concerning for a right-sided carotid dissection. The imaging modality of choice to detect a carotid dissection is CTA and MRI/MRA of the head/neck. The patient has a severe contrast allergy to iodinated contrast; therefore, CT/CTA is contraindicated, which makes MRI/MRA the correct answer. Gadolinium is not an iodinated contrast dye, and patients with an allergy to iodinated dye are not likely to be allergic to gadolinium. Carotid ultrasonography can detect some cases of carotid dissection, but is not the imaging modality of choice, because of its inferior sensitivity. PET is helpful for detecting occult malignancy, but it is not used for diagnosing carotid dissection.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What test is the most sensitive means of detecting abnormal visual function in a patient with papilledema?
pool.rationale: With acute papilledema, optic nerve function, including visual acuity and color vision, is usually normal. Pupillary responses are also normal; visual field tests may demonstrate only enlargement of the blind spot. Optic nerve function can deteriorate in patients with chronically elevated intracranial pressure and long-standing papilledema. With chronic papilledema, visual field defects can include nasal field loss, arcuate scotomata, and generalized peripheral depression. Central visual field involvement with decreased visual acuity typically does not occur until late.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What complication following third cranial nerve (oculomotor) palsy is suggestive of a nonischemic cause?
pool.rationale: Aberrant regeneration may develop after congenital or traumatic third cranial nerve palsy, but does not after ischemia. Aberrant regeneration most commonly produces eyelid retraction in downgaze, eyelid elevation or pupil constriction on attempted adduction, and globe retraction on attempted upgaze. Aberrant regeneration does not occur with ischemic causes, which include diabetes mellitus, hypertension, atherosclerosis, and migraine.

pool.q: A 35-year-old man has vertical, binocular diplopia that seems worse when driving. He has a left hypertropia of 5 PD in primary gaze, absent on right gaze, increasing to 9 PD on left gaze with clockwise gaze-evoked nystagmus. There is no head tilt. What additional finding on examination would help to support the most likely diagnosis?

options.c: proptosis of right eye greater than left

pool.rationale:
This patient has an incomitant left hypertropia (worse in left gaze) and gaze-evoked nystagmus. The hypertropia does not follow a cranial nerve pattern, and the presence of nystagmus suggests a supranuclear disorder such as skew deviation. Skew deviation may occur with internuclear ophthalmoplegia in a young person who has demyelinating disease, and in an older person may result from ischemia. Given the left hypertropia, the lesion causing the skew deviation is most likely on the left side of the brainstem; the hallmark of a left internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) would therefore be slowed adduction saccadic velocity in the left eye.
Both thyroid eye disease (which can cause proptosis) and ocular myasthenia gravis (which can cause fluctuating ptosis) may cause the same ocular deviation (left hypertropia worse in left gaze), but would not produce the nystagmus. Increased vertical fusional amplitude is seen most commonly with longstanding cranial nerve (CN) IV palsy or other vertical strabismus and would not be expected in this patient, whose strabismus does not fit that pattern.

pool.q: Slit-lamp examination of a large pupil that is minimally reactive to light reveals vermiform movements. The pupil reaction is slow to near stimulus. The patient has no ptosis, and ocular motility is normal. Where is the responsible lesion located?

options.b: fascicular portion of cranial nerve III

pool.rationale:
The findings are characteristic of damage either to the iris sphincter muscle or its innervation from the parasympathetic system, as in Adie tonic pupil. Herpes zoster can give this same picture.
Lesions at the dorsal midbrain also produce light near dissociation, but findings are bilateral and not vermiform in terms of constriction.
Fascicular CN III lesions should give either ptosis and/or a motility deficit along with the pupil dilation, and vermiform movements are again not present.
Sympathetic denervation at the second-order neuron (ciliospinal center) leads to Horner syndrome with a miotic pupil.

pool.q: A 39-year-old woman has had episodic diplopia for 2 years. Ductions are normal, and there is no ptosis. Alternate cover testing shows a 12 prism diopter, intermittent left hypertropia in primary position that increases to 25 prism diopters on right gaze and downgaze; it decreases to 3 prism diopters in upgaze and left gaze. She has a right head tilt and becomes diplopic on left head tilt. What additional finding is most likely to accompany this condition?

options.a: unilateral or bilateral proptosis with conjunctival chemosis and redness
options.b: rapid resolution of strabismus after injection of pyridostigmine
options.c: documentation of a right head tilt in a photograph taken at age 18
options.d: periventricular white matter lesions on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery [FLAIR] sequence)

pool.rationale:
This patient has a strabismus pattern consistent with left fourth nerve palsy (left hypertropia worse on right gaze and left head tilt). She is able to fuse a 12 prism diopter vertical deviation, which represents an abnormally high fusional amplitude. This can develop in adults but usually results from a longstanding vertical strabismus such as congenital or childhood trochlear nerve (CN IV) palsy. Even minor head trauma can cause CN IV palsy, and the condition may not become symptomatic until later in adulthood, when the well-controlled strabismus starts to break down. Old photos frequently show a compensatory head tilt being present for many years before the diplopia started.
A patient with a newly acquired CN IV palsy in adulthood would not be able to fuse the deviation measured here. While myasthenia gravis can mimic a CN IV palsy, that is less likely here because of lack of ptosis and chronicity without any change. Thyroid eye disease causes restrictive strabismus, and ductions would not be normal. Multiple sclerosis (MS) rarely causes cranial nerve palsies.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What imaging method is preferred to identify calcium in an orbital lesion?
pool.rationale: CT scan is optimal for analysis of calcium in lesions, such as meningiomas. MRI is a less effective and more expensive option for visualizing calcium. PET scanning would not be a cost-effective technique for visualizing intralesional calcium. Gamma ray-emitting radionuclides such as technetium-99 do not provide comparable anatomical details to contrast imaging, but they may be useful for evaluating obstructions of the tear ducts.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with oscillopsia worse in downgaze. Examination demonstrates downbeat nystagmus, which follows Alexander's law. If a causative structural lesion is present, what is the most likely location of the lesion?
pool.rationale:
Downbeat nystagmus is the most common form of central vestibular nystagmus. It results from lesions that produce defective vertical gaze holding, characterized by an upward drift, then correction with a downward saccade. Lesions that cause downbeat nystagmus compromise the vestibulocerebellum (including the nodulus, uvula, flocculus, and paraflocculus) and decrease the tonic output from the posterior semicircular canals to the ocular motor neurons. According to Alexander's law, the downbeating movements are accentuated in downgaze. Patients usually report oscillopsia.
If there is a structural lesion causing the downbeat nystagmus, then it most commonly is located at the cervicomedullary junction. The most common causative lesion is a Arnold-Chiari I malformation, a developmental abnormality characterized by posterior fossa crowding and cerebellar tonsillar protrusion into the foramen magnum.
A lesion of the dorsal midbrain may produce a Parinaud syndrome, characterized by upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze, mid-dilated pupils with light-near dissociation, eyelid retraction, skew deviation, disruption of convergence, and increase square-wave jerks.
A lesion of the sella may produce a bitemporal hemianopia secondary to chiasmal compression and, rarely, a see-saw nystagmus.
A lesion of the lateral medulla may produce a Wallenberg syndrome, characterized by ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature sensation, contralateral loss of body pain and temperature sensation, ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, ipsilateral first-order Horner syndrome, and ipsilateral ocular tilt reaction.

pool.q: What structure lies adjacent to the fascicles of cranial nerve III?
pool.rationale: The portion of cranial nerves that courses within the brainstem is called a fascicle. The fascicles of the cranial nerves will pass adjacent to other major structures. Lesions within these areas will result in specific clinical syndromes that help to localize the lesion to a specific area of the brainstem. Cranial nerve III (oculomotor nerve) passes adjacent to the superior cerebellar peduncle, cerebral peduncle, red nucleus, substantia nigra, and corticospinal tracts. Lesions in these areas may cause Nothnagel syndrome (superior cerebellar peduncle), Benedikt syndrome (red nucleus and substantia nigra), Weber syndrome (cerebral peduncle), and Claude syndrome (superior cerebellar peduncle and red nucleus). Cranial nerve IV (trochlear nerve) courses below the pineal gland; large pineal tumors may cause CN IV palsies. The nucleus of cranial nerve VI (abducens nerve) lies below the fourth ventricle and its fascicles pass medial to the superior olivary nucleus.

pool.q: A patient with myasthenic strabismus and ptosis returns for examination 5 years after diagnosis via a single fiber electromyography (EMG). The patient currently has no systemic manifestations of generalized myasthenia. What is the likelihood of progression to generalized disease?

options.b: moderate risk of progression until 10 years
options.c: high risk because of positive single fiber EMG test

pool.rationale: Up to 20% of patients who present with isolated ocular myasthenia gravis (MG) (no systemic weakness) may progress to generalized MG, but this typically occurs in the first 2 years. This patient is at low risk for generalized MG because the manifestations have remained purely ocular for 5 years.

pool.q: A 56-year-old woman presented with a long-standing 4th nerve palsy. Prior records show that initially she had a 15 prism diopter (PD) right hypertropia (RHT) in primary position, 10 PD RHT in right gaze and 25 PD RHT in left gaze. On your examination, the deviation measures 15 PD in all directions. What process occurred to explain this?
pool.rationale: An incomitant deviation may become comitant with the passage of time, which is called spread of comitance. Suppression is an adaptation that occurs in early onset strabismus. It reduces the responsiveness of the visual neurons in the occipital cortex to the input from 1 eye to avoid symptoms of diplopia. Vergence is the simultaneous movement of both eyes in opposite directions to maintain single binocular vision. Convergence is a type of vergence where the eyes rotate toward each other to look at a near object.

pool.q: A 62-year-old patient presents with a left facial droop, left abduction deficit, and numbness over the left side of the face. There was no weakness of the arms or legs noted on examination. What part of the brainstem is most likely affected?
pool.rationale:
The clinical vignette describes a left cranial nerve (CN) V, left CN VI, and left CN VII palsy without body weakness. This is most consistent with Foville syndrome, in which intra-axial lesions of the CN VI fascicles also injure CN VII fascicles, the tractus solitarius, and the descending tract of CN V. This results in an ipsilateral abduction palsy, facial weakness, loss of taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and facial hypoesthesia.
The CN VI nucleus lies within the dorsal caudal pons, and dorsal lesions to the pons can cause Foville syndrome, whereas lesions of the ventral pons can damage CN VI and CN VII, along with the corticospinal tract, which results in contralateral hemiplegia, ipsilateral facial weakness, and abduction deficit. This is called Millard-Gubler syndrome

pool.q: A 49-year-old patient presents with a central scotoma and optic disc pallor in the right eye and a superotemporal visual field defect with a normal-appearing optic disc in the left eye. What diagnostic test is the best next step in evaluation?

options.a: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy genetic test
options.b: erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein tests
options.c: vitamin B12, folate, copper, thiamine levels
options.d: magnetic resonance imaging of the brain

pool.rationale:
The clinical scenario describes a patient with a junctional scotoma (optic neuropathy in 1 eye and a superotemporal visual field defect in the other eye) that localizes to the anterior chiasm.
Non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) is a diagnosis of exclusion that typically presents with unilateral vision loss in the setting of optic disc edema. The optic disc edema should resolve within 2 months, with subsequent development of optic disc pallor (either diffuse or sectoral). The visual field defect typically persists in NAION, although the density of the defect may improve. A temporal visual field defect in the contralateral eye would not be explained by NAION. Although giant cell arteritis should be considered in patients with suspected bilateral optic neuropathy, the patient's age makes giant cell arteritis much less likely. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy and toxic-nutritional optic neuropathies typically present with central or cecocentral visual field defects. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy may be unilateral, sequential, or bilateral in presentation. Toxic-nutritional optic neuropathies are bilateral in presentation and typically symmetric, with a similar appearance to both optic nerves. Vitamin B12, folate, copper, and thiamine deficiencies have been implicated in nutritional optic neuropathy.

pool.q: A 28-year-old woman with new blurred vision at near has anisocoria with the left pupil being larger and reacting poorly to direct or consensual stimulus. With sustained reading, the left pupil constricts and then redilates slowly. What systemic finding may sometimes be associated?
pool.rationale:
This patient has light-near dissociation and tonic constriction of the left pupil with sustained near stimulus. The most likely diagnosis is Adie pupil (idiopathic tonic pupil), which may occur in the context of Adie syndrome with decreased or absent deep tendon reflexes. Patients with Adie syndrome are much more likely to have bilateral simultaneous or sequential eye involvement. While Horner syndrome in the eye with the smaller pupil, in this case the right, must be considered, the presence of light-near dissociation on the left identifies it as the abnormal pupil.
Urinary incontinence may be seen with many neurological disorders, such as MS and normal pressure hydrocephalus, and these conditions are not associated with the pupil findings seen here. Palmar rash can occur with acquired syphilitic infection, especially in secondary syphilis. Decreased facial sweating (facial anhidrosis) is a characteristic of Horner syndrome.

pool.q: What is the initial surgical correction for heavy eye syndrome?

options.b: bilateral loop myopexy between the inferior and medial rectus muscles
options.d: bilateral loop myopexy between the superior and lateral rectus muscles

pool.rationale: Heavy eye syndrome occurs in the setting of high myopia, causing superotemporal prolapse of the posterior globe. This displaces the superior rectus muscle medially and the lateral rectus muscle inferiorly, causing limited supraduction and abduction of the eye. Bilateral loop myopexy between the superior rectus muscle and lateral rectus muscle restores the normal anatomic configuration. All the other surgical options listed (bilateral medial rectus muscle recession, bilateral lateral rectus muscle resection, bilateral loop myopexy between the inferior and medial rectus muscles) would not restore the normal anatomic configuration, thus leading to a suboptimal surgical outcome.

pool.q: What drug has been most commonly associated with the condition that could cause mental status changes and hemianopsia in a patient with multiple sclerosis (MS)?
pool.rationale: Altered mental status in the presence of a hemianopic visual field defect raises concern for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a condition associated with natalizumab in patients who are John Cunningham (JC)-virus positive. The other therapies have either not been associated or been associated with encephalopathy only in rare cases. Fingolimod can cause macular edema.

pool.q: Twenty-four hours after uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a healthy 8-pound girl, a 24-year-old woman presented with bilateral visual loss and severe headaches. She had pregnancy-induced hypertension, which was under good medical control, and proteinuria. Dilated eye examination was unremarkable. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed bilateral occipital lobe white matter hyperintensity on T2 sequences. What is the most likely cause of her vision loss?
pool.rationale:
This patient is most likely suffering from posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). PRES is characterized by headache, altered mental status, seizures, and visual disturbances (transient visual loss, scotomata, photopsias, dimming of vision); MRI shows edema involving the white matter of the cerebral posterior regions, especially parieto-occipital lobes. PRES can be caused by acute hypertension, and preeclampsia/eclampsia, and can be seen in the postpartum period. The abnormalities visible on neuroimaging are reversible, and the visual prognosis is usually excellent.
Neither idiopathic intracranial hypertension nor anterior ischemic optic neuropathy would  explain the occipital lobe T2 hyperintensities, and in both cases, there would be findings of optic disc edema. Stroke is less likely here, given the classic presentation of PRES.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 56-year-old woman has slowly progressive diplopia. In primary gaze, she has partial ptosis, a mid-dilated pupil, exotropia, and hypotropia of the right eye. In attempted adduction, the right eyelid rises and the pupil constricts. What would be a likely cause for her examination findings?
pool.rationale:
This patient is showing signs of a right third nerve palsy, as indicated by the ptosis, mydriasis, and the down and out eye position. In addition, the elevation of the eyelid and constriction of the pupil in adduction indicates the presence of aberrant regeneration, which can occur after damage to the nerve and is due to misrouting of fibers that regrow to innervate muscles other than those they original innervated. Classic findings include eyelid retraction with adduction or pupillary miosis with elevation, adduction, or depression.
The other answer choices (demyelinating third nerve palsy, congenital third nerve palsy, ischemic third nerve palsy) can cause or mimic a third nerve palsy, but only a compressive etiology would be expected to result in aberrant regeneration. A cavernous sinus meningioma or carotid aneurysm in the cavernous sinus are common lesions responsible for compressive third nerve palsies. Aberrant regeneration is common after trauma or compression by an aneurysm or tumor, but it is rarely seen in a third nerve palsy caused by microvascular ischemia or ophthalmoplegic migraine. This is because the nerve sheath typically needs to be disrupted for aberrant regeneration to occur.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 70-year-old man with a history of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy in the right eye 5 years prior presents for his annual follow-up examination. His acuity remains 20/20 in the affected eye. Humphrey visual field shows a stable inferior altitudinal defect. What pattern would be expected on the optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan of the retinal nerve fiber layer?
pool.rationale:
OCT is a powerful tool for the evaluation of patients with optic neuropathies, and a growing body of literature suggests that measurement of retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) or macular integrity can be a surrogate for overall disease severity. In a patient with a prior nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), the degree and site of RNFL (and ganglion cell complex) thinning often correlates with the threshold sensitivity of the corresponding area of the visual field. Since this patient has an inferior field defect, we would expect the corresponding superior retinal nerve fiber layer to be thinned.
Diffuse thickening of the RNFL may be present in an acute NAION but will not be present months or years later.
A normal RNFL would not be expected in a nerve that has experienced an ischemic insult, leaving the patient with a residual visual field defect.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 75-year-old male presents with abnormal eye movements. He appears to be unable to glance at objects to the right but is able to track a finger in all directions of gaze. What part of the brain may be affected?
pool.rationale: Saccadic eye movements are generated by the frontal eye fields, located in the frontal lobe, one on each side. Each frontal eye field initiates saccades to the contralateral side. Smooth pursuit eye movements are generated by the medial temporal (MT) visual area (V5) in the parietal lobe, and each area generates smooth pursuit eye movements to the ipsilateral side. The inability to initiate saccades is called ocular motor apraxia and may be present in childhood in several conditions or may be acquired as a result of injury to the frontal lobe. Patients with ocular motor apraxia thrust their heads to establish fixation on their object of interest and use their vestibulo-ocular reflex to compensate for the inability to initiate saccadic movements. In this patient, the inability to look to the right suggests damage to the left frontal eye field, located in the left frontal lobe.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 55-year-old male with a history of diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obstructive sleep apnea awoke with painless vision loss in his left eye. He had no vision changes in the right eye. Examination showed hyperemic disc edema and peripapillary hemorrhages in the left eye. What nerve appearance would be expected in the right eye?
pool.rationale:
In a 55-year old man, the most common cause of acute painless vision loss upon awakening is nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), especially in the setting of vascular risk factors. NAION is associated with the following risk factors: structural crowding of the disc (disc-at-risk), systemic hypertension, diabetes mellitus, obstructive sleep apnea, and hyperlipidemia. NAION presumably relates to compromised optic disc microcirculation in eyes with structural “crowding” of the disc.
A cupped nerve would be suggestive of glaucoma, bilateral optic nerve swelling would be concerning for papilledema, and a pale nerve would indicate a prior optic neuropathy, none of which are consistent with this clinical scenario.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Approximately what percentage of patients with acute isolated demyelinating optic neuritis have eye pain?
pool.rationale:
Acute isolated demyelinating optic neuritis is the most common form of optic neuritis. It typically presents in young white women and is characterized by subacute unilateral painful vision loss over 1 to 3 days. Examination findings include decreased visual acuity, visual field defects, dyschromatopsia (especially red-green) significantly worse than loss of visual acuity, and relative afferent pupillary defect (if unilateral). The optic nerve is edematous in 35% (papillitis) and appears normal in 65% (retrobulbar optic neuritis).
According to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT), 92% of cases have periorbital pain, especially with eye movement. This eye pain often precedes the visual loss by 1 to 2 days. The ONTT noted that the eye pain typically improves after 3 to 5 days; eye pain lasting more than 1 week is considered atypical for optic neuritis. It is theorized that the eye pain is worse with eye movements due to the proximity of the annulus of Zinn (especially with the superior and medial recti muscles) to the inflamed optic nerve sheath dura.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 57-year-old man has been experiencing intermittent diplopia as well as lid droopiness over the past 3 weeks. His symptoms are worse in the afternoon and evening and seem to improve after a good night’s rest. He does not report any trouble speaking, swallowing, or breathing. What laboratory testing is most useful to establish a diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The correct answer is acetylcholine receptor binding antibody. Binding antibodies are most commonly requested, since they are detected in almost 90% of patients with generalized myasthenia gravis and 50% of patients with ocular myasthenia. The patient in this case needs serologic testing to evaluate for ocular myasthenia gravis.
Blocking antibodies are usually requested when the binding antibody is negative. Blocking antibodies are rarely present (1%) when the binding antibody is absent. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are most commonly associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis and are not commonly drawn in the initial workup for myasthenia gravis. Anti-muscle specific kinase (MuSK) antibodies can sometimes be detected in patients who do not have anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, but they are not detected more frequently than binding antibodies. Neuromyelitis optica antibodies can be found in Devic disease or neuromyelitis optica.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 52-year-old woman has transient, painless vertical binocular diplopia lasting for seconds. It is accompanied by an odd sensation in her right eye when it occurs. What finding on slit-lamp examination of the right eye during an episode is most consistent with these symptoms?
pool.rationale:
The patient is reporting symptoms suspicious for superior oblique myokymia, which is characterized by monocular, paroxysmal, high-frequency bursts of superior oblique contraction. The resulting eye movements are of very small amplitude and usually require magnification (such as at the slit lamp or with a 20 D lens) for observation.
Many conditions, including ocular myasthenia gravis and decompensated phorias, may produce fleeting double vision. In these cases, patients do not experience the tremulous ocular sensation that is present with superior oblique myokymia. The diagnosis may be challenging unless an episode is observed, and high clinical suspicion is required once alternative diagnoses are excluded with motility and cover testing. Phacodonesis should not cause diplopia, nor would anterior chamber shallowing. Pulsatile proptosis is usually constant and thus rarely causes transient diplopia as noted here.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 28-year-old woman reported having a small left pupil for the past few weeks. She denied ptosis, diplopia, or pain. In light, her pupils were 6 mm OD and 3 mm OS. In a dim setting, her pupils were 6 mm OD and 4.5 mm OS. What investigation is most likely to yield useful information?

options.b: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the neck with fat suppression

pool.rationale:
Although she complains of the small left pupil, this patient presents with anisocoria worse in light than dark, indicating a problem with iris sphincter constriction in light and thus the parasympathetic nervous system in the larger pupil. (See Figure 1, Flowchart for evaluation of anisocoria.) A dilated, poorly reactive pupil, in the absence of ptosis or motility dysfunction, is consistent with idiopathic tonic (Adie) pupil. (Idiopathic tonic pupil is known as Adie pupil.) Additional characteristics of Adie pupil include light-near dissociation (poor reaction to light but strong pupillary response to near), sectoral palsy of the iris sphincter, and supersensitivity of the short ciliary nerves to parasympathomimetics such as pilocarpine. (See Figure 2, Sectoral palsy of iris sphincter in Adie pupil. The sphincter is paralyzed between the 7 o’clock and 9 o’clock sectors [arrows].) While normal pupils would be expected to constrict to 1% pilocarpine, only the Adie pupil will constrict to 0.1% dilute pilocarpine.
Cocaine 10% is a test for Horner syndrome, not Adie pupil.
MRI of the neck with fat suppression would be appropriate as part of the work up of Horner syndrome. Adie pupil is generally benign and does not raise concern for compressive mass, aneurysm, or dissection.

pool.q: In a patient with an acute optic neuropathy, what symptom suggests the arteritic form?
pool.rationale: Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy causes isolated, sudden, permanent vision loss, often preceded by or associated with episodes of transient visual loss or episodes of transient diplopia.

pool.q: A young man presents with recurrent episodes of transient monocular visual loss in the right eye following a car accident. He also reports experiencing ipsilateral headache. What clinical finding is highly suggestive of a right internal carotid artery dissection?
pool.rationale: An acute painful Horner syndrome is highly suggestive of an ipsilateral internal carotid artery dissection, especially in a patient with recurrent episodes of transient monocular visual loss. Hemiparesis contralateral to the eye involved or retinal emboli in the affected eye both suggest a possible internal carotid artery stenosis, but these findings are not specifically suggestive of dissection. Diplopia should be expected with vascular events in the posterior circulation.

pool.q: In a patient with Adie tonic pupil, what pupillary reaction is typically observed in the affected eye after sustained near viewing?

options.d: stable pupil size with vermiform movements

pool.rationale: Adie pupils have poor light reaction but develop a tonic constriction to near stimulus. This effect may last several seconds after viewing the near target; then the pupil will slowly return to its baseline size over several seconds. The dilation may not occur evenly; however, the vermiform movement that accompanies the initial constriction is not part of redilation. The Adie pupil does not exhibit hippus (alternating constriction and dilation).

pool.q: What tool can be used to quantify relative afferent pupillary defects (RAPDs)?
pool.rationale:
Neutral density filters can be used to quantify a RAPD. The filters come in 0.3 log unit strengths.  The amount of RAPD can be quantified by placing increasingly stronger filters in front of the normal eye to decrease the intensity of the light stimulus until there is no RAPD on the swinging light test.
The Pelli-Robson chart is a contrast sensitivity visual acuity chart.  Bagolini lenses are used to test for strabismus and anomalous retinal correspondence. The red-green duochrome test is used to refine a manifest refraction.

pool.q: An obese and asymptomatic 15-year-old girl is found to have optic disc abnormalities. B-scan echography shows normal retrobulbar optic nerve size and refractile bodies beneath the disc surface. What management is recommended for this patient?

options.b: optic disc photos and visual field monitoring
options.c: intravenous methylprednisolone, 1 gram daily for 3 days
options.d: magnetic resonance imaging of the orbits

pool.rationale:
This case describes a young patient with optic disc drusen (ODD), which represent refractile, often calcified nodules located within the optic nerve head.
When buried beneath the retinal nerve fiber layer (NFL), they crowd the optic disc and elevate the retinal NFL, mimicking true optic nerve edema (ie, pseudopapilledema). They demonstrate hyperechoic signal on B-scan or CT.
ODD can cause visual field defects similar to those of glaucoma, and they tend to be nonprogressive. There is no proven treatment to prevent visual loss, and the prognosis is usually very good.
Acetazolamide is a first-line agent in treating idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), which causes true papilledema (optic nerve head edema from increased intracranial pressure).
Intravenous steroid is the initial treatment of choice for acute optic neuritis.



(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: A 70-year-old diabetic man presents with an acute left head turn and a left mouth droop, but no diplopia. What is the most likely etiology?

options.c: Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome

pool.rationale:
This case describes a patient with a left gaze palsy, as indicated by the compensatory left head turn. Many of these patients do not have diplopia because the sixth nerve nucleus contains 2 populations of motoneurons: (1) those that innervate the ipsilateral lateral rectus, and (2) those that travel via the medial longitudinal fasciculus to innervate the contralateral medial rectus. In addition, the mouth droop indicates facial palsy from 7th nerve fascicle fibers that wrap around the 6th nerve nucleus prior to exiting the pons.
Other diagnoses such as myasthenia gravis and the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome can present with a variety of motility complaints and facial weakness, but an ischemic lesion of the pons in this 70-year-old vasculopathic man is most likely.
A cavernous sinus lesion would be expected to produce a peripheral abducens nerve palsy, not lateral gaze palsy, and would not affect the facial nerve.

pool.q: A 34-year-old previously healthy woman has painless blurred vision OS for 10 days. She has visual acuity of 20/40 OS, a left afferent pupillary defect (APD), and a central scotoma OS on perimetry. The left optic nerve is minimally swollen, with stellate lipid encircling the fovea. What diagnostic procedure should be performed?

options.a: lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement
options.b: fundus autofluorescence (FAF) and enhanced depth imaging (EDI)
options.c: urgent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain and orbits with gadolinium contrast
options.d: serologies for T pallidum, B henselae, and B burgdorferi

pool.rationale:
T pallidum, B henselae, and B burgdorferi

This patient has a constellation of findings typical for neuroretinitis, including mild vision loss, disc swelling, and a star pattern of lipid in the fovea. Common causes include Bartonella henselae/cat scratch disease, syphilis, and Lyme disease, and patients should be screened for infections and possible treatment. Papilledema severe enough to cause vision loss and foveal exudate within 10 days should be much greater than seen here, so lumbar puncture would not be the desired first step. MRI is not indicated for neuroretinitis. FAF and EDI rarely provide additional diagnostically useful information in patients with neuroretinitis.

pool.q: What type of eye movements are primarily affected in ocular motor apraxia?
pool.rationale: As described by Cogan, congenital ocular motor apraxia is idiopathic and is characterized by increased latency and intermittent failure of horizontal saccadic initiation. Vertical eye movements are normal.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Gaze-evoked transient monocular visual loss is indicative of what condition?
pool.rationale:
Gaze-evoked transient monocular visual loss (TMVL) is classically associated with an orbital tumor that is either large or located in the orbital apex, such as a hemangioma or meningioma. The TMVL likely results from a combination of direct compression of the optic nerve and ischemia from positional vascular obstruction. Careful examination usually reveals other orbital findings, such as proptosis or limited ocular motility.
The visual loss of optic neuritis is not gaze dependent. However, pain with eye movement is a common feature.
Visual loss from papilledema can be exacerbated by body position. Patients often complain of transient visual obscurations when standing up from a sitting position.
Visual loss from optic disc drusen (ODD) can be progressive, but is not gaze-induced; up to 75% of patients with ODD can develop visual field defects, usually peripheral. Transient visual loss akin to that occurring in papilledema can also occur with ODD. Peripapillary hemorrhages, ischemic optic neuropathy, and retinal vascular occlusions are also sequelae of ODD.

pool.q: A 41-year-old female presents for evaluation of double vision. She reports that her double vision persists with occlusion of the left eye but resolves with occlusion of the right eye and is present in all directions of gaze. Her ductions and versions are full, and she does not have any deviation noted on cover testing. Her corrected visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. What diagnostic test is the most appropriate next step for this patient?

options.c: optical coherence tomography of the macula

pool.rationale: The clinical vignette is describing monocular diplopia (diplopia present in one eye), which typically results from abnormalities of the refractive media. The use of a pinhole to resolve the diplopia proves an optical etiology and obviates the need to pursue neurological workup. Corneal topography is appropriate in the workup of some cases of monocular diplopia (eg, keratoconus), but is not necessary in all cases of monocular diplopia. OCT of the macula may help uncover retinal pathology, but retinal pathology does not commonly cause monocular diplopia. Edrophonium is used in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis and would not be indicated in the workup for monocular diplopia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 40-year-old woman had sudden onset of severe headache, diplopia, and decreased vision in both eyes. Examination shows bilateral ptosis, poorly reactive pupils, and ophthalmoparesis. What abnormality is most likely to be present on neuroimaging of the head and orbits?
pool.rationale:
The constellation of bilateral vision loss, ophthalmoparesis, and ptosis shows involvement of multiple cranial nerves as well as the optic nerves in the pathological process. Tumors or other skull base disorders can give all of these findings, either unilaterally or bilaterally. The sudden onset with headache should create suspicion for pituitary apoplexy, where rapid tumor expansion with hemorrhage causes compression of the chiasm and/or optic nerves as well as cranial nerves in the cavernous sinuses.
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm should give unilateral findings without vision loss, since the optic nerve is not compressed. Internal carotid artery dissection in the cavernous sinus can give cranial nerve paresis, again without vision loss and almost always unilaterally. Demyelinating disease presents in a less acute, and rarely painful, manner.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Aberrant regeneration of the third nerve without a history of third nerve palsy indicates a lesion in what location?
pool.rationale:
Aberrant regeneration, also known as oculomotor synkinesis, is a well-described phenomenon frequently resulting from trauma, tumors, or aneurysms. It is rare in microvascular disorders. Aberrant regeneration without a history of CN 3 palsy, which is called primary aberrant regeneration, is presumptive evidence of a slowly expanding parasellar lesion, most commonly a meningioma or carotid aneurysm within the cavernous sinus, which requires appropriate neuro-imaging.
The 6th nerve is vulnerable in the prepontine space. Fistulas can develop between the carotid and the cavernous sinus. A posterior communicating artery aneurysm can also cause a 3rd nerve palsy but not with primary aberrant regeneration.

pool.q: What magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) sequence would be best for detecting the demyelinating lesions associated with multiple sclerosis (MS)?
pool.rationale: Both active and inactive demyelinating lesions are best detected with FLAIR images. FLAIR provides T2-weighted images without the high (bright) CSF signals, making this imaging modality ideal for detecting periventricular white matter lesions in a demyelinating process such as MS. Only active lesions may be seen with T1/contrast images, and DWI is insensitive for MS. T2, though similar to FLAIR in some respects, is still less sensitive for detecting white matter lesions as seen in MS because a bright signal from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) may mask some lesions.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What horizontal movement is preserved in one-and-a-half syndrome?

options.a: adduction of the eye opposite the lesion
options.b: abduction of the eye on the side of the lesion
options.c: abduction of the eye opposite the lesion
options.d: adduction of the eye on the side of the lesion

pool.rationale: One-and-a-half syndrome is a condition in which a pontine abnormality is of sufficient size to involve both the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) and the cranial nerve (CN) VI nucleus (or the adjacent paramedian pontine reticular formation [PPRF]) on the same side. This results in a combination of a unilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) and a horizontal gaze palsy. If the lesion is on the right side, the PPRF/nuclear lesion would impair gaze to the right side for both eyes. Because the MLF on the right side carries fibers from the left CN VI nucleus that ultimately will stimulate the right medial rectus, adduction of the right eye is also impaired. As a result, the right eye has no horizontal movement at all (the "one") and the left eye has impaired adduction (the "half"). The only preserved horizontal movement in one-and-a-half syndrome is abduction on the side opposite the lesion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: During automated static perimetry, a false positive represents what response?

options.a: the patient does not respond to a light brighter than the pre-determined threshold at that location
options.b: the patient blinks during presentation of a light stimulus.
options.c: the patient responds to a light stimulus presented in the blind spot
options.d: the patient responds but no light stimulus is displayed

pool.rationale:
During automated static perimetry testing, reliability is assessed using several indices. A false-positive error is recorded when the patient responds but the perimeter presents no light stimulus: a rate of less than 25% on threshold testing and less than 15% on the Swedish interactive threshold algorithm (SITA) testing is considered acceptable.
A false-negative error occurs when the patient fails to respond to a light of greater intensity than the determined threshold for that spot, with an acceptability rate of less than 25% (keeping in mind that the incidence will increase in areas of true visual field loss).
When the patient responds to a stimulus presented in the blind spot, it is a fixation loss because the patient's blind spot is presumed to have moved from the previously plotted area into the seeing eye field.
A patient blinking during presentation of a light stimulus will cause the gaze-tracking strip to deflect off of the midline and may result in a false-negative error.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: With regard to the pupil exam, what is light-near dissociation?

options.a: when the pupil responds to bright light at near but not dim light at near
options.b: when the bright light response exceeds the near response
options.c: when the bright light response produces anisocoria but the near response does not
options.d: when the near response exceeds the bright light response

pool.rationale: Light–near dissociation is demonstrated when the near response exceeds the best constriction that bright light can produce. Care should be taken to provide appropriate accommodative targets, and a lack of near response usually indicates that the patient isdissociation not trying hard enough. The other scenarios are not consistent with light-near dissociation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the appropriate length for a temporal artery biopsy in the evaluation of giant cell arteritis?
pool.rationale: Due to the possibility of skip lesions, it is possible to miss the diagnosis with small specimens of temporal artery. Thus, a negative biopsy does not rule out giant cell arteritis (GCA). In fact, false negative biopsy rates are believed to be anywhere from 3% to 9%. To avoid a false negative result, it is recommended to obtain a specimen at least 2-3 cm in length. In cases where the degree of suspicion for GCA is high but the initial temporal artery biopsy is negative, biopsy of the contralateral temporal artery may be undertaken. Once GCA is suspected, temporal artery biopsy should be done expeditiously, but it is generally accepted that performing the biopsy within 1 week of starting steroid therapy will not compromise the histopathological diagnosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with convergence retraction nystagmus after a stroke. What is the most likely associated finding?
pool.rationale:
Convergence-retraction nystagmus is a feature of the dorsal midbrain syndrome. Also known as the pretectal or Parinaud syndrome, dorsal midbrain syndrome includes some or all of the following findings: conjugate limitation of vertical gaze (usually upgaze), co-contraction of extraocular muscles with attempted upgaze (convergence-retraction nystagmus), mid-dilated pupils with light–near dissociation, retraction of the lids in primary position (Collier sign), skew deviation, disruption of convergence (convergence spasm or convergence palsy), and increased square-wave jerks.
Limitation of conjugate upgaze is the most common feature and occurs with damage to the pretectum, an isthmus between the superior colliculi and the thalamus. Supranuclear fibers decussate through the pretectum as they pass to the rostral interstitial nucleus of medial longitudinal fasciculus (riMLF), the midbrain structure that functions as the saccadic generator for vertical eye movements.
Comitant esotropia, monocular elevation deficit, and apraxia of eyelid opening are not the correct answers because they are not part of the dorsal midbrain syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 78-year-old man presents with acute difficulty doing simple math, difficulty writing, inability to recognize his fingers, and left-right confusion. These symptoms are typical of a stroke involving what part of the brain?
pool.rationale: The correct answer is the dominant parietal lobe. Gerstmann syndrome is defined by acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, and left-right confusion, and it occurs with damage to the dominant parietal lobe. Other signs of parietal lobe damage include contralateral homonymous hemianopias or contralateral inferior quadrantanopias or optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) abnormalities due to damage to the pursuit pathways in targets moving toward the lesion. Disorders of attention, including hemispatial neglect, also occur with nondominant parietal lobe involvement.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What pharmacologic agent is used to confirm the diagnosis of Horner syndrome?
pool.rationale:
Horner syndrome (figure) can be confirmed with cocaine drops. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine released at neuromuscular junctions of the iris dilator muscle. Following instillation of cocaine in the normal eye, the pupil will dilate. In Horner syndrome, whether pre- or postsynaptic, the pupil dilates poorly because there is little or no norepinephrine being released into the synaptic cleft. Hydroxyamphetamine can be used to localize the lesion producing Horner syndrome to preganglionic or postganglionic. Hydroxyamphetamine will dilate the pupil in a normal eye or in a preganglionic Horner syndrome (because the postganglionic neuron is intact). In a postganglionic Horner syndrome the nerve terminal has degenerated and the pupil will dilate poorly. Norepinephrine and epinephrine are not used pharmacologically in the diagnosis or evaluation of Horner syndrome.

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)
