pool.q: A 30-year-old man has bilateral ptosis and an adduction deficit of the left eye from myasthenia gravis (MG). What would an examination of his pupils most likely reveal?

options.a: bilateral constricted pupils with poor constriction and poor redilation
options.b: bilateral dilated pupils with poor pupillary constriction
options.c: normal pupillary function with normal constriction and normal redilation
options.d: dilated left pupil with poor pupillary constriction in the left eye

pool.rationale:
Although MG can cause eyelid ptosis and ocular motility disorders of almost any pattern, pupillary abnormalities and sensory disturbances are not associated with MG, and their presence should provoke a search for another diagnosis. Thus, a patient with known ocular MG should demonstrate normal pupillary function on examination.
The other options, which describe dilated or constricted pupils with poor function, would suggest an efferent pupillary disorder, such as unilateral or bilateral Adie tonic pupil if noted in isolation, or third cranial nerve palsy or Horner syndrome with eyelid findings.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What test is indicated after examining a 15-year-old female who has bilateral ptosis, limited ductions, and pigmentary retinopathy?
pool.rationale:
Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) is an inherited mitochondrial myopathy that causes slowly progressive, symmetric limitation in extraocular muscles (EOM) and ptosis with weakness of the orbicularis oculi muscles. CPEO and pigmentary retinopathy in a young patient should raise concern of Kearns-Sayre syndrome, a triad of CPEO, pigmentary retinopathy with visual field loss, and heart block. It is therefore important to order an EKG and consider involving cardiology.
Audiogram and otolaryngology consultation would be indicated in the management of Usher syndrome (retinitis pigmentosa and congenital neurosensory hearing loss).
Lumbar puncture and neurology consultation would be indicated in the management of suspected multiple sclerosis, which can cause optic neuritis and/or ocular motility disorders.
Renal imaging and urology consultation would be indicated in a patient with foveal hypoplasia from aniridia due to WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary malformation, and mental retardation).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What cranial nerve passes below the petroclinoid ligament to enter the cavernous sinus?
pool.rationale: Cranial nerve VI starts at its nucleus in the dorsal base of the pons, exits the pons anteriorly, ascends along the clivus, crosses the petrous apex, and passes below the petroclinoid ligament to enter the cavernous sinus, where it runs between the lateral wall and the carotid artery. Because of this 90 degree turn over the tip of the clivus and under the petroclinoid ligament, it is poised for brain compression from abnormally high or low intracranial pressure, causing bilateral VI nerve palsies. CN III, CN IV, and CN V (V1) have a separate course through the subarachnoid space and into the cavernous sinus.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common pattern of color confusion associated with acquired color vision defects?
pool.rationale:
Acquired color vision defects are most frequently blue-yellow or tritan abnormalities; they affect females and males equally. Blue-yellow color defects often accompany an optic neuropathy but also can occur in a maculopathy.
Hereditary color vision defects are most frequently red-green abnormalities. They are most often X-linked recessive and affect 5%-8% of males and 0.5% of females.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common primary tumor of the optic nerve?
pool.rationale: Optic pathway gliomas are uncommon, accounting for only about 1% of intracranial tumors. However, they are the most common primary tumor of the optic nerve. Optic pathway gliomas are more common in children, with 90% of tumors detected by the second decade of life.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: If a patient has a left Horner syndrome with anhidrosis limited to the left forehead, what structure must the lesion be at or distal to?
pool.rationale: A lesion of the oculosympathetic pathway occurring anywhere from the hypothalmus to the pupillary dilator muscle will result in Horner syndrome. Anhidrosis of the ipsilateral head, face, and neck  occurs with first or second order Horner syndrome, whereas anhidrosis limited to the ipsilateral forehead occurs with a lesion at or distal to the superior cervical ganglion (third order Horner syndrome).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What optic nerve finding is most characteristic of dominant optic atrophy?

options.b: yellow peripapillary halo with ring of pigmentation

pool.rationale: Dominant optic atrophy typically presents before age 10, with visual acuity ranging from 20/40 to 20/100. Visual fields show a central or cecocentral scotoma with normal peripheral isopters. Color vision reveals a blue dyschromatopsia (tritanopia). Clinically, the optic disc shows temporal pallor with an area of triangular excavation. Superotemporal or inferotemporal notching is characteristic of glaucoma. Peripapillary telangiectasia is a characteristic of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON). A yellow peripapillary halo with a ring of pigmentation is characteristic of optic nerve hypoplasia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Resting pupil size is influenced by several factors, including ambient light, level of arousal, patient age, and neurologic disease. What typically causes small pupils?
pool.rationale: Extremely small pupils suggest pontine hemorrhage, narcotic intoxication, or pilocarpine use.  Pupils typically become smaller as a result of age. Elevated intraocular pressures and anxiety can lead to larger pupils.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a clinical feature of Adie tonic pupil?
pool.rationale:
Adie tonic pupil is a parasympathetic denervation of the pupillary sphincter resulting in a fixed (tonic) and dilated pupil. Because the denervation is segmental, there can be sectors of the iris that still constrict, but not to the same degree as a normal contralateral pupil. This results in anisocoria that is more pronounced in bright light. Because the parasympathetic innervation of the ciliary muscle may also be affected, accommodative insufficiency, not spasm, may occur, resulting in blurred vision. Because the afferent visual pathway is uninvolved, there is no relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus-Gunn pupil) despite the unequal parasympathetic tone to the pupillary sphincter muscles. The parasympathetic fibers associated with the light reflex are affected more than those for the near response; this results in light-near dissociation. Adie tonic pupil, when associated with decreased deep tendon reflexes, is called Holmes-Adie syndrome.

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 65-year-old pseudophakic woman presents with loss of central vision over 3 weeks in her right eye. Best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) is 20/200 OD, 20/30 OS, a trace right relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is present, color vision is impaired OU, and visual fields show central scotoma OD only. She complains of flashes in her central vision bilaterally, with worsening night vision. Fundus exam appears normal OU. What clinical test is most likely to be abnormal in this setting?
pool.rationale:
This clinical scenario is most consistent with an autoimmune or paraneoplastic retinopathy, not optic neuropathy, due to the photopsias and nyctalopia described. While MRI orbit may be considered with a clinical optic neuropathy, the electroretinogram (ERG) would be most likely to reveal photoreceptor dysfunction in this case. Optical coherence tomography of the macula (OCT) may show disruption of the ellipsoid zone in the outer retina. While serum testing for antibody to recoverin (23kD protein) is the most common anti-retinal antibody associated with cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR), it is not present in the majority of cases. Thus, patients with occult retinopathies revealed on multifocal and/or full-field ERG should undergo evaluation for underlying malignancy to exclude paraneoplastic retinopathies such as CAR and MAR, which may mimic optic neuropathies.
Aquaporin-4 IgG antibody disease, or neuromyelitis optica (NMO), usually presents as a severe unilateral or bilateral optic neuritis and may have a similar presentation, but would be less likely to create photopsia and nyctalopia and should have a larger right RAPD, possibly with pain on eye movement. In addition, other areas of the optic pathway, brainstem, and cervical spine may be concurrently affected in NMO.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the smallest diameter of cerebral aneurysm detectable by high-quality magnetic resonance angiography?
pool.rationale: Current computed tomographic angiography or magnetic resonance angiography techniques reliably detect cerebral aneurysms of at least 3 mm diameter.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What feature characterizes the mydriasis caused by Adie pupil?

options.a: quick redilation on looking from near to far distances

pool.rationale:
Mydriasis caused by neurologic disease such as Adie pupil (idiopathic tonic pupil) is easily overcome with instillation of full-strength or even dilute pilocarpine.
Damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves produces an Adie pupil, which is characterized by a large pupil with poor reaction to light but a strong and tonic pupillary response to near vision (light-near dissociation). The pupil experiences a slow tonic redilation on looking from near to far distances. Stromal thinning is observed in areas of sphincter paralysis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 31-year-old woman had subacute painful vision loss to counting fingers in the right eye that recovered over the subsequent 3 months. One year later, visual acuity is 20/30 OD, 20/20 OS with a trace right relative afferent pupillary defect and minimal right optic disc pallor. Visual evoked potential test results show markedly delayed P100 latency in both eyes. What abnormality is most likely present on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain?

options.a: gadolinium enhancement of both optic nerves
options.b: non-enhancing tumor compressing the optic chiasm
options.c: periventricular white-matter lesions on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences

pool.rationale:
This patient initially presented with a right optic neuritis and later was shown to have an abnormal visual evoked potential (VEP) in both eyes.
Abnormalities on VEP testing may indicate optic nerve dysfunction and can suggest an etiology. The most common wave measured in VEP testing is the P100 wave. Reduced amplitudes are less specific than is delayed P100 latency, which typically is seen with demyelinating optic neuropathies.
Based on the history of optic neuritis and the evidence of bilateral optic nerve demyelination based on VEP, there is concern for multiple sclerosis. Therefore, central nervous system (CNS) white-matter lesions may be present as well. Asymptomatic demyelination, as may be present in this patient, can be diagnosed when the P100 latency is severely delayed.
Compressive and ischemic lesions do not usually cause such marked change to the P100 latency, although they may affect P100 amplitude. Optic nerve enhancement should not be seen with disease that was active 1 year prior.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 45-year-old man presents with several episodes per day of severe left-sided orbital and temporal pain that lasts 5–10 minutes, occasionally associated with left ptosis and miosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Paroxysmal hemicrania is a form of trigeminal autonomic cephalgia associated with short bouts of pain highly responsive to indomethacin. Although cluster headache is also unilateral and frequently associated with autonomic features, the bouts of excruciating pain are of longer duration (15–180 minutes). Hemicrania continua is characterized by a continuous unilateral headache. Idiopathic stabbing headache manifests as episodic, very brief, sharp, jabbing pains, unassociated with autonomic features.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 50-year-old female patient presents with an intermittent electric shock-like pain in her right forehead and cheek. She has noticed her symptoms seem to be precipitated by wind on her face. Her examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Trigeminal neuralgia usually occurs in middle-aged patients and is described as a paroxysmal burning or electric-shock type pain in the face, lasting seconds to minutes. It can be primary or secondary, with the majority of cases caused by vascular compression of cranial nerve V (CN V). In primary trigeminal neuralgia, the pain usually involves CN V2 or V3 distribution unilaterally. Involvement of CN V1 distribution only is suggestive of a secondary cause. The facial pain may be precipitated by chewing, tooth brushing, or cold wind on the face. Examination is normal in primary trigeminal neuralgia. Occipital neuralgia by contrast causes a paroxysmal stabbing pain in the distribution of the greater or lesser occipital nerves. There is usually tenderness to palpation over the affected nerve. Temporomandibular disease pain may be referred to the ear, preauricular region, or neck. There may be a click or pop upon jaw opening. Internal carotid artery dissection usually produces unilateral facial pain and is often associated with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Optociliary shunt vessels are a feature of what entity?
pool.rationale:
Orbital meningiomas originate in the arachnoid of the optic nerve sheath. They most commonly occur in women in their third and fourth decades of life. Symptoms include gradual, painless, unilateral loss of vision. Examination findings may include decreased visual acuity; relative afferent pupillary defect; proptosis; ophthalmoplegia; normal, atrophic, or swollen optic nerve head; and visible optociliary shunt vessels (also identified as "tortuous vessels").
Orbital cavernous hemangiomas also occur more commonly in women. They are the most common benign neoplasm of the orbit. Findings include progressive proptosis, retinal striae, hyperopia, optic nerve compression, increased intraocular pressure, and strabismus. Orbital fibrous dysplasia is a benign developmental disorder of bone. Computed tomography (CT) shows hyperostotic bone. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows lack of dural enhancement, which distinguishes fibrous dysplasia from meningioma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 10-year-old boy with a recent history of otitis media presents with fever, lethargy, and headache. Ocular examination reveals bilateral disc edema. What diagnostic procedure would be most helpful?
pool.rationale: This child presents with signs and symptoms of meningitis, which is diagnosed clinically and supported by the presence of increased white blood cell count in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), as well as changes in CSF protein, glucose, and cultures. Lumbar puncture (done after neuroimaging) to collect CSF is the most helpful diagnostic procedure. Neuroimaging is usually obtained prior to lumbar puncture to rule out large mass lesions, and blood testing with cultures also helps in associated sepsis management, but orbital MRI, CT angiography, and chest radiography are unlikely to be initially helpful.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 49-year-old woman complains of blurred vision in her left eye. On examination, her right eye is normal. Her left eye has visual acuity of 20/40 and an afferent pupillary defect. The left eye also has a deficit of adduction, elevation, and abduction, and levator function of 10 mm. What management should be initiated?

options.a: Hospitalize the patient for intravenous corticosteroid and temporal artery biopsy.
options.b: Order complete blood cell (CBC) count with differential, gastrointestinal (GI) workup, and anti-GQ1b antibody titers.
options.c: Obtain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits with contrast.
options.d: Perform rest/ice testing in the office, with edrophonium testing if negative.

pool.rationale:
This patient has signs of orbital apex syndrome with a left optic neuropathy, ptosis, and limited ductions. Temporal arteritis does not give insidious symptom onset; therefore, it is unlike the case here and is very unlikely in a 49-year-old person. Because there is also an optic neuropathy, diseases like Guillain-Barré syndrome (and its Miller Fisher variant) and myasthenia gravis (MG) are also unlikely, as they do not cause optic nerve dysfunction. An MRI of the brain and orbit is needed to look for orbital apex pathology and possible intracranial spread.



(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What nerve courses along the surface of the clivus?
pool.rationale: The abducens nerve (CN VI) exits the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle and courses anteriorly over the clivus and underneath the petroclinoid (Gruber) ligament to enter the Dorello canal. Lesions within the clivus and certain skull base fractures may damage the abducens nerve in this location. The oculomotor nerve and trochlear nerve course above the clivus for most of their subarachnoid course to enter their dural canals near the clivus as they pass into the cavernous sinus. The trigeminal nerve courses extra-axially before entering the dura near the petrous pyramid.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 48-year-old woman suddenly develops painful vision loss in her right eye. Two weeks later, she develops similar symptoms in her left eye. She is counting fingers with the right eye and hand motion with the left eye, without a relative afferent pupillary defect, but with sluggishly reactive pupils. Her dilated exam in the right eye is normal, but she has mild optic nerve head (ONH) edema in the left eye. MRI shows bilateral enhancement of the optic nerves. After treatment with IV methylprednisolone, she experiences only minimal vision recovery. What underlying condition is the most likely cause of her bilateral vision loss?
pool.rationale: This vision loss is most consistent with bilateral optic neuritis. The bilateral nature of the vision loss, along with the severity of visual impairment and minimal recovery after treatment, raise a concern for neuromyelitis optica. It is uncommon for MS to present with bilateral optic neuritis with minimal recovery. Giant cell arteritis can cause bilateral severe vision loss associated with headache, but it does not affect young patients. Fingolimod has been associated with macular edema, which would cause blurred vision, but not this degree of vision loss.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 18-year-old woman reports tunnel vision in both eyes. Visual acuity is 20/400 OU, pupils react briskly, and anterior and posterior segments are normal. She is able to ambulate without difficulty. What finding on Goldmann perimetry confirms a nonorganic component to her vision loss?
pool.rationale:
The disparity between visual acuity and examination result raises suspicion for nonorganic vision loss. In Goldmann kinetic perimetry, the visual field is tested continuously in a clockwise or counterclockwise direction, starting with the (smallest) I4e stimulus. A common nonorganic response shows a spiraling isopter getting closer and closer to fixation as testing continues. As larger stimuli are employed, there is often further constriction, resulting in overlapping isopters.
A step across the vertical or horizontal midline (eg, nasal step) may indicate at least some physiologic component to the field abnormality.
Central scotomata may occur in many disease processes, such as toxic or nutritional optic neuropathy or Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, and are not suggestive of nonphysiologic disease.
While generalized field constriction can occur in the setting of nonphysiologic visual loss, it also can occur in disease processes such as retinitis pigmentosa. Generalized constriction does not confirm nonorganic vision loss.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For 3 days, a 67-year-old man has had difficulty reading with his right eye. Visual acuity is normal, but he has an inferior altitudinal visual field defect, superior optic disc swelling, and a small peripapillary hemorrhage. In taking the patient's recent history, what question could reveal a risk factor for the most likely ocular disorder?

options.a: Do you snore and wake frequently while sleeping?
options.b: Do you have a tendency to bleed excessively?
options.c: Do you have episodic right-sided headache with tearing and eye redness?
options.d: Have you had evening drooping of the upper eyelid?

pool.rationale:
The most common cause of acute acquired optic neuropathy in adults is nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). Patients with NAION classically have inferior altitudinal visual field defects with superior optic disc edema and peripapillary hemorrhages. Sleep apnea is a risk factor for NAION. NAION is also associated with structural crowding of the disc (strongest risk factor), diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.
Thrombophilia, not hemophilia, is a proposed risk factor for NAION. Episodic right-sided headache with tearing and eye redness is suggestive of a cluster headache, which is associated with Horner syndrome, not NAION. Evening drooping of the upper lid could suggest myasthenia, which would be unrelated to NAION.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most frequent cause of a complete, pupil-sparing cranial nerve III palsy?
pool.rationale:
Microvascular disease is the most common cause of a complete, pupil-sparing cranial nerve III palsy. The parasympathetic pupillary fibers are located in the periphery of the nerve at its superonasal aspect and are thought to be spared the deeper ischemic insult seen in microvascular disease (hypertension, diabetes, etc.) in many cases. In contrast, an expanding posterior communicating artery aneurysm compresses the third nerve preferentially at its periphery, resulting in pupillary involvement.
Blunt head trauma and demyelinating disease can result in oculomotor nerve palsy, but they are far less frequent etiologies than ischemia. Of note, traumatic third nerve palsy typically requires significant intracranial trauma with associated neurologic injury,
Two other issues regarding third nerve palsy are worth mentioning. First, the "rule of the pupil" applies only to complete third nerve palsy. A partial (evolving) third nerve palsy—regardless of pupillary involvement—should be treated with the same urgency as a pupil-involving complete third nerve palsy: An expanding aneurysm may cause only partial involvement of the oculomotor nerve early in the process.
The second issue is work-up of third nerve palsy. All partial or pupil-involving complete third nerve palsies are considered emergencies and require urgent neuroimaging including noninvasive angiography. While urgent neuroimaging may not be required in a complete, pupil-sparing third nerve palsy in an older patient with vascular risk factors, many ophthalmologists and neuro-ophthalmologists choose to image all third nerve palsies to avoid missing dangerous pathology.

pool.q: A 76-year-old man has worsening constant diplopia over 6 months. He has a history of excised left-sided facial squamous cell carcinoma and diabetes mellitus. Examination reveals 3 mm left ptosis and reduced left eye motility. His right eye moves normally. Numbness of his left cheek is found on examination. What is the most likely cause of his diplopia?
pool.rationale:
Constant left-sided ptosis and ophthalmoplegia suggests cranial nerve (CN) III palsy. Ipsilateral facial numbness indicates CN V2 lesion. The most common location for multiple CN palsies is the cavernous sinus, and differential diagnosis is broad. Given a history of facial malignancy, anesthesia of CN V2 suggests recurrence of squamous cell carcinoma with perineural spread into the cavernous sinus. Perineural spread usually indicates malignant tumor such as adenoid cystic carcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma, as in this case.
Sympathetic chain denervation would not lead to dysmotility.
Uncontrolled type II diabetes mellitus causes an ischemic, not slowly progressive, CN palsy. An opportunistic cavernous sinus infection secondary to uncontrolled diabetes, such as mucormycosis, would be expected to progress rapidly, have other findings such as necrotic nasal debris, and render the patient acutely ill.
ICA aneurysm would not account for the presence of CN V and CN VI palsy.

pool.q: A 65-year-old man with polymyalgia rheumatica presents for evaluation of transient vision loss. He has recently experienced pain when chewing and tenderness when combing his hair. An urgent workup for what disease is indicated?

options.d: embolic occlusion of the ophthalmic artery

pool.rationale: Approximately 10% of patients with polymyalgia rheumatica eventually develop the vasculitis underlying GCA. Symptoms include jaw claudication and scalp tenderness. Optic nerve insult may result from GCA; it is an ischemic event rather than an inflammatory etiology, as in some other causes of optic neuritis. GCA can be associated with retinal arterial occlusions, but an embolic workup is not usually indicated. Cavernous sinus syndrome would present with orbital apex impairment symptoms including ophthalmoplegia and proptosis.

pool.q: A patient who has multiple sclerosis and a past history of a single severe episode of optic neuritis in her right eye that resulted in a relative afferent pupillary defect after resolution presents with equally round and reactive pupils with no afferent pupillary defect. What is the most common cause of the above finding in this patient?

options.b: cortical cataract in the left eye
options.c: optic neuritis in the left eye
options.d: recurrent optic neuritis in the right eye

pool.rationale:
A patient who has had an episode of severe right optic neuritis in the past would be expected to have a relative afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the right eye. However, if the patient developed damage of a similar magnitude to the other optic nerve, then the patient would be expected to have "loss" of the APD. In this patient, optic neuritis in the left eye would result in "loss" of the right afferent pupillary defect if the degree of optic nerve involvement matched that in the right eye. It is important to remember the term "relative" when thinking about afferent pupillary defects, which detect the amount of light perceived by the optic nerve. If both optic nerves are equally damaged, then the amount of light perceived by each is similarly decreased and there is no relative difference between them to produce an APD. An APD is most commonly seen with processes affecting the optic nerve and is very sensitive at detecting asymmetries in optic nerve conduction.
Although an APD can be caused by pathology other than that affecting the optic nerve (large retinal detachments, for example), the most common cause of an APD is optic nerve pathology. Recurrent optic neuritis in the right eye would worsen the relative afferent pupillary defect. A cataract will not cause loss of the right RAPD. Transient visual changes brought on by exercise (Uhthoff sign) occur despite recovery from the initial optic neuritis episode and do not affect the appearance of the APD. Therefore, this is not helpful in regard to possible optic neuritis in the left eye. In this scenario, loss of the APD is most suggestive of an optic neuritis or optic nerve damage in the left eye.

pool.q: What is the preferred order of surgical procedures for a patient with severe thyroid eye disease that requires multiple surgeries?

options.a: orbital decompression, eyelid surgery, strabismus surgery
options.b: strabismus surgery, orbital decompression, eyelid surgery
options.c: orbital decompression, strabismus surgery, eyelid surgery
options.d: eyelid surgery, strabismus surgery, orbital decompression

pool.rationale: Orbital decompression will often alter or augment pre-existing strabismus, so it should always precede strabismus surgery. Similarly, the strabismus surgery often alters the position of the eyelids, particularly the inferior eyelids. Eyelid surgery should be the last step.

pool.q: What component of the ocular exam is more suggestive of an optic neuropathy than of a maculopathy?
pool.rationale: A large relative afferent pupillary defect is highly suggestive of unilateral or asymmetric optic neuropathy (although CRAO and CRVO an also cause large APDs). A small relative afferent pupillary defect can be seen with significant asymmetric retinal damage involving the macula. Color vision can be altered in patients with maculopathies or optic neuropathies. A central scotoma might be seen in both maculopathies and optic neuropathies. Mild optic nerve head pallor is common in numerous chronic retinopathies such as cone dystrophies.

pool.q: A 24-year-old obese white woman with a body mass index (BMI) of 41 presents with a few seconds of vision blurring with spontaneous recovery, headache, and a "swooshing" sound in her ears. She is found to have mild papilledema and a normal magnetic resonance imaging/magnetic resonance venography (MRI/MRV) result. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 45 cm of water. What features of her presentation are associated with poor prognosis?
pool.rationale: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) is a disease in which 90% of patients are women who are obese, and it peaks in the third decade of life. It presents with signs and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure. Common symptoms include headaches that are worse when lying down, transient visual obscurations, and pulsatile tinnitus. Visual field testing, along with acuity and color testing, are mandatory to evaluate visual status and determine further treatment. MRI/MRV and lumbar puncture are used to rule out other causes of increased intracranial pressure such as a mass, dural sinus thrombosis, or meningitis. Poor visual prognosis is associated with male gender, African American race, morbid obesity (a BMI of 40 or more), anemia, and severe papilledema.

pool.q: What clinical sign is expected in patients with bilateral fourth cranial nerve (CN IV) palsies?
pool.rationale: The superior oblique muscle intorts, depresses, and abducts the eye. A patient with a bilateral CN IV palsy presents with crossed hypertropia (right hypertropia on left gaze and left hypertropia on right gaze), extorsion of at least 10°, a large V-pattern esotropia (esotropia greatest on downgaze), and chin-down positioning (as hypertropia decreases in upgaze). Intorsion of the hypertropic eye accompanies a skew deviation in the ocular tilt reaction.

pool.q: What percentage of patients with idiopathic isolated peripheral CN VII palsy (Bell palsy) spontaneously improve?
pool.rationale:
Bell palsy refers to an isolated, unilateral, peripheral dysfunction of cranial nerve (CN) VII that causes an acute hemifacial paresis. Approximately 85% of patients with Bell palsy experience a satisfactory spontaneous recovery. Subtle signs of aberrant regeneration can be detected on examination. Recovery typically begins within 3 weeks of onset of the deficit and is complete by 2-3 months. In the remaining patients, recovery is incomplete, and significant synkinesis with co-contraction of a variety of facial muscles is common. Complete facial palsy at the time of presentation, impairment of lacrimation, dysacusis, pregnancy, diabetes mellitus, and advanced age are all poor prognostic factors.
Although facial numbness has been reported, a true decrease in cutaneous facial sensation would suggest concurrent CN V involvement. CN V involvement, bilateral facial weakness at onset, and elevated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) white count, should prompt a workup for secondary causes of facial palsy, such as infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic etiology.

pool.q: A 47-year-old man noted difficulty reading with his left eye. His visual acuity was 20/40 in the left eye, 20/20 in the right. Humphrey visual field testing showed a central scotoma in the left eye and superotemporal loss in the right eye. Neuroimaging showed a lesion affecting the afferent visual system. Where would the lesion be located?
pool.rationale: This patient has a junctional scotoma with central loss in the ipsilateral eye and a temporal hemianopia in the opposite eye. This is caused by a lesion compressing the optic nerve at its junction with the anterior optic chiasm. Posterior chiasmal compression typically causes a bitemporal hemianopia. Optic tract lesions and lateral geniculate nucleus lesions cause homonymous hemianopia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most important reason that magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should not be performed on a patient with a metallic foreign body in the eye?

options.a: potential for dislodging the metallic foreign body
options.b: overestimation of the size of the metallic foreign body

pool.rationale: The magnetic field can dislodge a metallic foreign body. In patients with intraocular metallic foreign bodies, this can result in severe damage to the eye. Exposure to ionizing radiation and lack of sagittal imaging are problems associated with computed tomography (CT) scans. Overestimation of vascular stenosis can occur with magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) scans.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Facial nerve palsy combined with hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction should prompt consideration of what diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
CPA lesions can result in a constellation of findings, including ipsilateral facial nerve palsy (upper and lower face), decreased tearing, dysgeusia, loss of salivary secretion, loss of taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, hearing impairment, nystagmus, vertigo, ataxia, and/or adjacent cranial nerve findings (CN V, CN VI).
Bell palsy is an isolated facial nerve palsy with no clear etiology. It is usually unilateral and is thought to be from inflammation or to be a sequela to herpes zoster infection.
The seventh cranial nerve is the cranial nerve most commonly involved in sarcoidosis. This sarcoidosis involves the parotid gland, which affects the facial nerve branches passing through this gland.
Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome is associated with recurrent unilateral or bilateral facial paralysis, accompanied by chronic facial swelling and lingua plicata (furrowing of the tongue). The etiology of this disorder, which usually begins in childhood or adolescence, is unknown. Of the listed answer choices, only a CPA mass would produce hearing and vestibular dysfunction in addition to a CN VII dysfunction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What clinical finding is consistent with aberrant regeneration of CN III?
pool.rationale: Aberrant regeneration of CN III occurs after damage results in regrowth and misrouting of fibers with innervation of muscles not normally activated together. This causes abnormal synkinetic phenomenon such as eyelid retraction with adduction or pupillary miosis with supraduction, adduction, or infraduction. Eyelid retraction with supraduction is a normal response to CN III activation. Aberrant regeneration of CN III is common after traumatic injury, but can also occur with compressive lesions such as aneurysms and tumors. Microvascular ischemic CN III does not cause aberrant regeneration.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: If the pupil affected by Horner syndrome fails to dilate with hydroxyamphetamine, where is the defect?
pool.rationale:
Hydroxyamphetamine acts to release norepinephrine from the presynaptic terminal. In the case of a normal eye or in a preganglionic Horner syndrome, the postganglionic neuron is usually intact, and one would expect normal dilation of the pupil. In a postganglionic lesion, the nerve terminal has degenerated, and the pupil will dilate poorly. Hydroxyamphetamine has no effect on pupillary muscles or their motor endplates

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: A 48-year-old woman with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome developed severe headache and diplopia over the past 2 weeks. On examination, she is 20/20 OU and has enlarged blind spots on automated visual fields. She has bilateral abduction deficits. Fundus examination reveals severe bilateral optic-disc swelling with hemorrhages. What diagnostic test should be performed next?

options.a: brain MRI and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)
options.c: brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV)
options.d: computed tomography (CT) scan of the head

pool.rationale:
The patient is presenting with classic signs and symptoms of raised intracranial pressure. Although the most common cause of raised intracranial pressure is idiopathic intracranial hypertension that affects young obese women, this is a diagnosis of exclusion only after neuroimaging and lumbar puncture have been performed to rule out an underlying cause.
Imaging is always performed prior to a lumbar puncture to ensure that no large mass is present that could possibly lead to brainstem herniation.
This patient has a history of anitiphospholipid antibody syndrome and has developed subacute onset of severe bilateral disc edema and bilateral abduction deficits, indicative of a fairly rapid increase in intracranial pressure. This is concerning for a possible cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, especially within the transverse or superior sagittal sinus, which often presents with signs and symptoms of raised intracranial pressure. Therefore, an MRV of the head is recommended to evaluate for a cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, in addition to an MRI brain scan to evaluate for other structural causes of raised intracranial pressure.
If the patient had a sudden onset of symptoms within the past day, a CT scan of the head would be appropriate to evaluate for intracranial hemorrhage. However, her symptoms have been present for the past 2 weeks, and therefore more detailed imaging with magnetic resonance is recommended to better evaluate for the cause. An aneurysm can present with headache, but it would be expected to cause other neurologic deficits if the patient had raised intracranial pressure from a ruptured aneurysm, and therefore an MRA is not warranted here.

pool.q: According to the results of the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT), what is the likely benefit of intravenous (IV) corticosteroid treatment in a patient with typical retrobulbar optic neuritis that started 5 days ago?

options.a: Visual function may recover more rapidly with treatment.
options.b: There is no benefit to prescribing this treatment.
options.c: Final visual acuity and contrast sensitivity will be improved.
options.d: Risk of progression to multiple sclerosis is reduced at 5 years.

pool.rationale: The ONTT enrolled patients with a first episode of optic neuritis who presented for evaluation within 8 days of symptom onset. Patients were randomized to intravenous corticosteroid treatment for 3 days, followed by oral prednisone for 11 days, oral prednisone for 14 days, or oral placebo. IV treatment was associated with more rapid visual improvement at 6 weeks after onset of symptoms, but final visual outcomes at 6 months were not statistically different amongst the 3 treatment groups. Analysis at the 2-year timepoint indicated that patients treated with IV steroids were less likely to progress to developing MS, but this effect did not persist even into the third year and was not observed after 5 years. The major predictor for risk of progression to MS was found to be the presence of one or more white matter lesions on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain.

pool.q: A 25-year-old individual has noticed episodes of intermittent vertical diplopia for several months. He has no history of recent injury or illness. Strabismus evaluation reveals a right hyperphoria in the primary position that increases on left gaze and on right head tilt. Fusional vertical amplitudes are 15 diopters. What next step would be helpful in arriving at the correct diagnosis?

options.c: neurological evaluation and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan

pool.rationale: The history and findings are consistent with a congenital superior oblique weakness. Old family photographs may reveal a longstanding compensatory head tilt. The large vertical fusional amplitudes help differentiate a congenital superior oblique weakness from a recently acquired onset. This distinction is important. If this were a recent onset of paresis and there was no history of trauma, a neurological evaluation and an MRI would be indicated. There are no associated signs that would indicate the individual has endocrine myopathy. There is no variability in the strabismus and no ptosis, which makes myasthenia gravis unlikely.

pool.q: A 79-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of difficulty chewing food, and of weight loss and headache. Her dentist recently diagnosed her with temperomandibular joint (TMJ) inflammation and prescribed ibuprofen. Over the past week, she has experienced transient visual loss in the left eye. The ophthalmologic examination is normal except for 1 cotton-wool spot in the left fundus. What is the best next step?

options.a: Obtain a computed tomography (CT) of the midface to rule out a parotid gland tumor as a cause for her TMJ disease.
options.b: Begin baby aspirin and obtain a carotid Doppler ultrasonogram and echocardiogram.
options.c: Stop the ibuprofen to minimize postoperative bleeding and schedule a temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks.
options.d: Obtain a Westergren sedimentation rate and begin systemic corticosteroids while awaiting the result.

pool.rationale:
The patient's clinical picture is highly suggestive of giant cell arteritis (GCA). GCA is an ophthalmologic emergency because of the potential for bilateral, irreversible visual loss. This patient is already visually symptomatic and has evidence of possible posterior segment ischemia (cotton-wool spot). The most important next step is the immediate initiation of appropriately dosed systemic corticosteroids, either orally or intravenously, along with initial serologic testing; in cases with a high suspicion for GCA, the results of serologic testing should not delay corticosteroid therapy. Serology usually includes the triad of Westergren sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and platelet count.
The gold standard for the diagnosis of GCA remains temporal artery biopsy (TAB), which can be safely performed in most patients even while anticoagulated. TAB should be performed as soon as possible, ideally within 2 weeks, but in some cases remains positive for months after the initiation of treatment.
While carotid stenosis may certainly present with amaurosis fugax, and carotid ultrasonography may in fact be necessary should the work-up for GCA prove negative, the leading diagnosis in this case remains GCA.
Jaw claudication can be misdiagnosed by clinicians as TMJ disease, but jaw or tongue claudication is the symptom most specific for GCA. This symptom should always be sought by the clinician in any patient over the age of 50 years with complaints of transient visual loss.

pool.q: At the end of his shift, a 25-year-old nurse has blurred near vision and is startled to discover that the right pupil is 8 mm, round, and not reactive to light or near stimulus. What response is expected after instilling 0.1% pilocarpine in both eyes?

options.a: the left pupil dilates to 8 mm
options.b: the right pupil constricts to 3 mm
options.d: both pupils remain the same size

pool.rationale: The patient's history, occupation, and the extremely large, unreactive pupil are all characteristic of pharmacologic mydriasis. In this case, the dilated pupil will not react to any concentration of pilocarpine. Dilute (0.1%) pilocarpine will constrict a dilated pupil in Adie syndrome, and 1% pilocarpine will constrict all but pharmacologically dilated pupils. Reversal of anisocoria occurs with apraclonidine testing for Horner syndrome.

pool.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with new-onset complaints of intermittent double vision for the last 6 months. On examination, double vision persists when covering the left eye, but disappears when covering the right eye and improves when the patient blinks. What diagnostic test is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Monocular diplopia is caused by aberrations in the optical system. It usually results from abnormalities of the refractive media. This can include uncorrected or irregular astigmatism, basement membrane dystrophy, tear film abnormalities, or cataract. Less commonly, monocular diplopia can result from macular pathology such as fluid, epiretinal membrane, or fibrosis.
Wavefront analysis will describe lower-order and higher-order optical aberrations but will not establish the etiology of the aberrations. Motility testing would be helpful in binocular diplopia. Macular pathology can cause double vision but would not be affected by blinking.

pool.q: After a first episode of optic neuritis in a patient, what is the best predictor for the future risk of multiple sclerosis (MS)?

options.a: enhancement of the optic nerve on orbital MRI
options.b: worsening of vision with exercise (Uhthoff phenomenon)
options.c: periventricular white-matter lesions on brain MRI
options.d: oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid

pool.rationale: An abnormal brain MRI scan showing at least one white-matter lesion consistent with demyelinating disease is the best predictor of MS in patients after a first episode of optic neuritis. The risk for developing MS is estimated at 72% after 15 years in patients with presence of abnormalities on MRI compared with about 25% in patients with normal brain MRI at presentation.

pool.q: Automated static perimetry has several indices to gauge the reliability of a visual field test. What reliability index measures how often the patient identifies the stimulus in the previously placed physiologic blind spot?
pool.rationale:
The reliability of perimetry results is assessed by identifying the following patient response characteristics:
  • Fixation losses: how often the patient identifies the stimulus in the previously plotted physiologic blind spot location (ie, a response not expected), indicating that the eye is not aligned with the fixation target.
  • False-positive response rate: how frequently the patient signals when no target is displayed.
  • False-negative response rate: how often the patient fails to signal when a target brighter than the previously determined threshold for that spot is displayed.
  • Gaze tracker: tracks the pupil and checks for eye movements, which are signaled as upward deflections, and blinks, which are signaled as downward deflections.

pool.q: A 75-year-old man with a history of hypertension presents to clinic after an episode of transient monocular vision loss, characterized by acute, painless vision loss in the right eye only, preceded by a descending curtain over the vision, which then resolved over 10 minutes. The episode occurred earlier that morning. Ocular examination is unremarkable. What is the best next step in management?

options.a: Check erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) and arrange outpatient follow-up.
options.b: Order urgent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain and orbits with contrast.
options.c: Evaluate immediately in the emergency department, preferably one associated with a stroke center.
options.d: Order computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the neck and echocardiogram as outpatient workup.

pool.rationale: In a patient of this age with transient monocular visual loss, 2 potentially devastating vascular causes must be evaluated immediately: (1) giant cell arteritis and (2) embolic phenomena. If an embolic cause is suspected, then a complete vascular and cardiac work up must proceed urgently, due to the increased risk of morbidity and mortality from stroke in this setting. Giant cell arteritis must also be ruled out in patients over age 50. Embolic evaluation must include (1) imaging of the carotid arteries (with Doppler, MRA, or CTA), (2) MRI with diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) to evaluate for associated cerebral ischemia, and (3) echocardiography to evaluate for valvular and cardiac wall defects, intracardiac tumors, and large thrombi. If a cardiac or carotid source for embolism is not found, then other systemic processes that could contribute to stroke must also be considered, including advanced age, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, smoking, and sleep apnea.

pool.q: Decreased levator function, lid lag on downgaze, and absent or poorly formed upper eyelid crease are characteristics of what condition?
pool.rationale: Decreased levator function, lid lag on downgaze, and absent or poorly formed upper eyelid crease are characteristics of congenital ptosis. CN III palsy causes ptosis with decreased levator function and there may be the appearance of lid lag on downgaze if there is aberrant regeneration causing lid retraction on downgaze, but there is no absent or poorly formed upper eyelid crease. Levator aponeurosis dehiscence is usually characterized by normal levator function and high upper eyelid crease. There is no lid lag on downgaze. Horner syndrome is characterized by normal levator function. The mild ptosis is due to denervation of the sympathetically innervated Müller muscle in the upper eyelid. The upper eyelid crease is normal and there is no lid lag on downgaze.

pool.q: What examination and/or ancillary test finding is most likely in a 40-year-old man with history of alcohol abuse and gastric bypass surgery who reports gradually progressive bilateral visual loss over a 4-month period?

options.d: cystoid macular edema on spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT)

pool.rationale: Gastric bypass surgery may lead to malabsorption of vitamin B12, and poor food intake with alcoholism may exacerbate this problem and lead to depletion of the body's vitamin B12 stores. This vitamin deficiency may cause optic neuropathy that primarily affects the papillomacular bundle and results in central vision loss with a cecocentral scotoma on visual field testing. Small pupils with light-near dissociation are seen with syphilitic infection or midbrain disorders, and are not associated with central vision loss. Optic disc swelling is not seen with nutritional deficiency. Macular edema, also, is not a consequence of poor nutritional intake, as seen in this case.

pool.q: What branch of the ophthalmic division of cranial nerve V  (V1) both supplies the tip of the nose and carries sensory fibers from the cornea?
pool.rationale: Sensory innervation to the area surrounding the orbit is provided by the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) divisions of the trigeminal nerve. The ophthalmic division (V1) further divides into 3 branches: the frontal, lacrimal, and nasociliary. These branches enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. In addition to supplying the sensory input to the nasal septum, turbinates, and tip of the nose, the nasociliary nerve branches into the long ciliary nerves that carry the sensory input from the cornea, ciliary body, and iris. The supraorbital nerve is a branch derived from the frontal nerve.

pool.q: A 65-year-old man has the gradual onset of diplopia. He has an esodeviation greater at distance than near. The deviation is equal in right and left gaze. Ocular motility is normal. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?

options.d: inferior displacement of lateral rectus muscles

pool.rationale:
This patient has divergence insufficiency. Divergence insufficiency is an esodeviation that is greater at distance than near. Primary divergence insufficiency, also known as age-related distance esotropia, is a benign condition that usually occurs in patients older than 50 years. The etiology is involution of the connective tissue band between the superior and lateral rectus, leading to inferior displacement of the lateral rectus muscles (sagging eye syndrome). Treatment consists of base-out prisms, botulinum toxin injection of the medial rectus muscle, or strabismus surgery.
There is a secondary form of divergence insufficiency that is rare and associated with neurologic abnormalities, such as pontine tumors, severe head trauma, or increased intracranial pressure. When present as an isolated finding, divergence insufficiency does not require further workup.
A sixth nerve palsy causes an esodeviation greater at distance than near, but the deviation is worse when looking to the side of the affected nerve. There is an abduction deficit. Elevated intracranial pressure and ischemia can cause sixth nerve palsies.

pool.q: A patient with a left face turn has absent left eye abduction with left globe retraction upon adduction. She denies diplopia. What brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) finding would be consistent with this clinical condition?

options.d: infarction of left sixth nerve nucleus

pool.rationale: Absent unilateral or bilateral abduction with globe retraction upon attempted adduction occurs in Duane syndrome. The left eye is more frequently affected, and the condition is more common in females. Duane syndrome is caused by a congenital maldevelopment or absence of the sixth nerve nucleus and/or nerve. A cavernous carotid aneurysm can cause sixth nerve palsy, but it will not produce globe retraction on adduction. A sixth nerve nucleus infarction results in a gaze palsy on the affected side. Lateral rectus aplasia will produce esotropia but not globe retraction on adduction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What visual field defect is most commonly found in cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR)?
pool.rationale:
Cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) is a paraneoplastic disease of the eye, associated with the presence of extraocular malignancy and circulating autoantibodies against retinal proteins. CAR is a subacute, progressive autoimmune retinopathy that induces visual loss and visual symptoms that often manifest before the diagnosis of cancer. The most common malignancies related to CAR are carcinomas including small cell carcinoma of the lung, non-small cell carcinoma, and endometrial, ovarian, cervical, breast, prostate, and colon carcinomas.
The most common visual field defect associated with CAR is the ring scotoma. The diagnostic evaluation should include electroretinography (ERG) in patients with unexplained visual glare and subacute visual loss, screening for anti-retinal antibodies associated with anti-recoverin (23-kDa protein) and anti-alpha-enolase (46-kDa) antibodies, and screening for systemic cancer.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What condition is visual evoked potential (VEP) testing most helpful in confirming?
pool.rationale: Visual evoked potential (VEP) testing measures electrical signals over the occipital cortex produced in response to a visual stimulus. It shows an increased latency in demyelination. Other optic neuropathies generally have a normal latency, but might show a decrease in the VEP's amplitude.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 64-year-old woman presents following an episode of transient vision loss in her right eye. Associated clinical history includes recent headaches, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness. Her vision and intraocular pressure are normal, and the clinical examination shows mild refractive error, but the anterior segment and fundoscopic examination results are otherwise normal. What clinical laboratory test is considered to be most specific in confirming the etiology?
pool.rationale:
This patient's clinical symptoms are highly suspicious for giant cell arteritis (GCA) or temporal arteritis. When evaluating patients whose clinical symptoms are suspicious for GCA, diagnostic testing should begin with laboratory tests of ESR, CRP, and CBC.
CRP is a sensitive indicator of inflammation and is typically obtained in conjunction with the ESR; however, the ESR may be normal in up to 16% of cases of GCA. CRP may increase diagnostic accuracy of GCA because it may be more specific and less affected by increasing age and anemia when compared to ESR.
CBC is obtained in order to evaluate for thrombocytosis (increased platelet count), which may suggest active disease, but is not specific to GCA.
Fasting blood glucose testing is useful to determine the etiology of clinical findings suggestive of diabetic retinopathy changes but has limited value in temporal arteritis.

pool.q: Following his final round of chemotherapy for leukemia, a 53-year-old man reports new diplopia and vision loss. His visual acuity is 20/200 OD, 20/20 OS with a right relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). He has ptosis and reduced motility OD. His fundus appearance is normal. What would be the most worrisome result from his sinus biopsy?

options.c: gram-positive cocci in clusters, resistant to methicillin

pool.rationale:
A biopsy demonstrating nonseptate fungal hyphae would indicate rhinocerebral mucormycosis, which typically occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus or in immunocompromised patients. The initial infection spreads from the facial skin, nasal mucosa, paranasal sinuses, or hard palate. The fungus spreads to the nearby blood vessels, affecting the orbital vessels, carotid arteries, cavernous sinuses, or jugular veins. Orbital and neurologic signs are produced by infarction, thrombosis, or hemorrhage. Untreated, rhinocerebral mucorrmycosis can lead to rapid deterioration, resulting in death within days.
This patient has vision loss and ophthalmoplegia, indicating an orbital apex syndrome. Patients with orbital apex syndrome from mucorrmycosis have nearly a 100% chance of permanent vision loss and > 60% mortality rate, despite aggressive surgical debridement and administration of antifungal agents.
Gram-positive cocci in clusters, resistant to methicillin, indicating methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), atypical mycobacterial infection, and granulomatous lesions with noncaseating centers, such as sarcoidosis, carry some risk of mortality and morbidity, but not to the extent of rhinocerebral mucormycosis.

pool.q: A 37-year-old man complains of new onset anisocoria. His right pupil is 4.0 mm, and his left is 3.0 mm. His right palpebral fissure is 11 mm, while his left is 9.5 mm. What test would confirm an oculosympathetic paresis on the left side?

options.a: anisocoria of 1 mm or more (left smaller than right) after instillation of apraclonidine drops OU
options.b: reversal of anisocoria after instillation of dilute pilocarpine drops OU
options.c: reversal of anisocoria after instillation of hydroxyamphetamine drops OU
options.d: anisocoria of 1 mm or more (left smaller than right) after instillation of cocaine drops OU

pool.rationale:
The patient has ptosis and a smaller pupil on the left indicative of a lesion to the oculosympathetic pathway, resulting in a left Horner syndrome. Other findings in a Horner syndrome are the presence of anisocoria that is greater in dim light than in bright light, dilation lag of the affected pupil, lower lid ptosis (rising of the lower lid), and anhidrosis of the ipsilateral face.
Horner syndrome can be confirmed with pharmacologic testing. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine released at sympathetic nerve terminals in the eye, causing pupillary dilation, eyelid retraction, and conjunctival blanching in the unaffected eye. With Horner syndrome, little or no norepinephrine is released into the synaptic cleft. Therefore, cocaine has no effect, and the miotic pupil remains unchanged. A postcocaine anisocoria of 1 mm or more is diagnostic of Horner syndrome on the side of the smaller pupil.
Topical apraclonidine can also be used to confirm Horner syndrome. A pupil with Horner syndrome will dilate in response to topical apraclonidine (weak alpha1-adrenergic agonist) because of iris dilator supersensitivity that develops several days after injury to the sympathetic pathway.
Hydroxyamphetamine testing can be used to localize a lesion after Horner syndrome is confirmed, but it is not helpful in diagnosing a Horner syndrome. Dilute pilocarpine is used to diagnose an Adie tonic pupil.

pool.q: A 41-year-old man has small, irregular, poorly reactive pupils on routine examination. The fundus has mild pigmentary changes. What additional testing should be performed?

options.a: herpes zoster polymerase chain reaction (PCR) evaluation

pool.rationale:
Treponema pallidum enzyme immunoassay (TP-EIA)

The Argyll Robertson pupil occurs in patients with tertiary syphilis involving the central nervous system. Affected patients have small pupils (< 2 mm) that are often irregular. The pupils do not react to light, but the near response and subsequent redilation are normal and brisk. This feature distinguishes Argyll Robertson pupils from bilateral chronic tonic pupils, which may also result from neurosyphilis. In addition, iris atrophy frequently occurs, portions of the iris transilluminate, and dilation is poor after instillation of mydriatic eyedrops.
Argyll Robertson–like pupils are observed in widespread autonomic neuropathies, such as bilateral tonic pupils (chronic), diabetes mellitus, and chronic alcoholism, as well as in encephalitis and after panretinal photocoagulation. Serologic tests for syphilis, such as the serum Treponema pallidum enzyme immunoassay (TP-EIA), fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test, rapid plasmin reagin (RPR), and Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test (VDRL), should be considered in the evaluation of patients with bilateral pupillary light-near dissociation with miosis, especially with retinal pigmentary changes.
Herpes zoster PCR evaluation tests for the varicella zoster virus, which does not cause Argyll Robertson pupils.
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for Borrelia burgdorferi tests for Lyme disease, which does not cause the Argyll Robertson pupillary response.
Quantiferon gold assay tests for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which does not cause the Argyll Robertson pupillary response.

pool.q: What is considered the gold standard for the evaluation of aneurysms or carotid stenosis?
pool.rationale:
The gold standard for intracerebral vascular imaging remains catheter angiography. With this technique, a catheter is placed intra-arterially, and iodinated radiodense contrast dye is injected. The contrast dye outlines the column of flowing blood within the injected vessel and demonstrates stenosis, aneurysms, vascular malformations, flow dynamics, and vessel wall irregularities such as dissections or vasculitis.
MRA and CTA have the advantage of being less invasive than catheter angiography. CTA requires injection of contrast material and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation, whereas MRA can be performed without any contrast material and does not involve any radiation exposure. While not considered the "gold standard," both CTA and MRA are technically adequate for detecting aneurysms that cause third nerve palsies.
Color doppler ultrasonography is primarily used in ophthalmology to evaluate for cervical carotid stenosis in patients presenting with transient monocular visual loss. Notably, it is not accurate at detecting carotid artery dissection.

pool.q: A 23-year-old man presents with a gradual loss of eye movements, pigmentary changes in the retina, and cardiac conduction abnormalities. What additional finding is expected on examination?
pool.rationale:
Kearns-Sayre syndrome is an inherited mitochondrial myopathy that includes chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO), pigmentary retinopathy, and cardiac conduction abnormalities. CPEO is characterized by slowly progressive, symmetric ophthalmoplegia often associated with bilateral ptosis.
Blepharospasm is typically seen in older patients and is not part of Kearns-Sayre syndrome. Variability is expected in myasthenia gravis. Improved eye movements with doll’s head maneuver indicate a supranuclear gaze palsy. Ophthalmoplegia associated with CPEO cannot be overcome with doll’s head maneuver.

pool.q: A patient presents with gaze-evoked nystagmus that dampens on prolonged right gaze. When returning to primary gaze, a left beat nystagmus ensues. Where is the lesion?
pool.rationale:
Gaze-evoked nystagmus occurs due to inability to maintain fixation in eccentric gaze. There is an ocular drift back to primary gaze as a result of the elastic properties of the orbit, and a corrective saccade to view the eccentric target. The amplitude of the nystagmus increases with eye movement in the direction of the fast phase. Gaze-evoked nystagmus is most commonly caused by the loss of neural integration.

Neural integration for horizontal gaze is mediated by the nucleus prepositus hypoglossi and the medial vestibular nuclei, whereas neural integration for vertical gaze is mediated by the interstitial nucleus of Cajal. The cerebellum is also involved in neural integration of horizontal and vertical gazes.

Rebound nystagmus is described in the above clinical scenario. Prolonged eccentric viewing causes compensatory brainstem/cerebellar induced-tonic innervation toward eccentric gaze, decreasing the amplitude of gaze-evoked nystagmus. However, when the patient returns to primary gaze, the tonic innervation continues to drive the eyes rightward, inducing a corrective leftward saccade. Gaze-evoked nystagmus with rebound nystagmus in primary gaze is frequently due to cerebellar disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 32-year-old woman has chronic headache that suddenly worsened 2 days ago. She cannot elevate either eye, and they move nasalward on attempted upgaze. She has bilateral disc edema and mild blind-spot enlargement by perimetry. What radiologically detectable finding would be expected in this clinical disorder?
pool.rationale:
This prompt describes convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze, a finding in dorsal midbrain syndrome (also termed pretectal syndrome or Parinaud syndrome). Dorsal midbrain syndrome is caused by compression of the posterior commissure, which controls horizontal conjugate eye movements. It includes any of the following findings: conjugate limitation of vertical gaze (usually upgaze), convergence-retraction nystagmus, mid-dilated pupils with light-near dissociation, lid retraction in primary position, skew deviation, convergence spasm or palsy, and increased square-wave jerks. Given the papilledema with enlarged blind spots bilaterally, there is likely increased intracranial pressure from a mass or hydrocephalus compressing the dorsal midbrain at the level of the pineal gland, associated with cerebral aqueductal stenosis.
Periventricular white-matter lesions are often seen in multiple sclerosis. Demyelination from multiple sclerosis can produce dorsal midbrain syndrome but would not cause papilledema and signs of increased intracranial pressure demonstrated in this case.
Transverse sinus thrombosis could cause increased intracranial pressure and papilledema but would not cause dorsal midbrain syndrome.
Occlusion of the vertebrobasilar artery that supplies the pretectum could cause dorsal midbrain syndrome, but it is not associated with increased intracranial pressure.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An ophthalmologist sees a patient whose examination results show an infiltrative optic neuropathy in association with leptomeningeal enhancement on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and an abnormal computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest. Bronchoscopic biopsy demonstrates noncaseating granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
pool.rationale:
Sarcoid optic neuropathy is a granulomatous inflammatory condition and can present as an infiltrative optic neuropathy. Hilar adenopathy on chest CT would raise suspicion of sarcoidosis, and biopsy demonstrating noncaseating granulomata is consistent with sarcoidosis. In cases of neurosarcoidosis, MRI scan commonly shows pachymeningeal and leptomeningeal enhancement. Corticosteroids and other immunomodulators like methotrexate and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) blockers are the mainstays of treatment.
While the imaging characteristics described in this case could be consistent with tuberculosis, characteristic pathologic findings include caseating granulomata (rather than the noncaseating ones of sarcoidosis). Lyme disease can present as an optic neuropathy without chest CT findings. It usually causes neuroretinitis with macular exudates in addition to optic disc edema. A CT chest would not be initially helpful in detecting syphilis infection.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What ocular motility abnormality is classically included in dorsal midbrain syndrome?
pool.rationale: The presence of convergence-retraction nystagmus localizes the disease process to the dorsal midbrain; it is part of dorsal midbrain syndrome (also known as pretectal or Parinaud syndrome). Convergence-retraction nystagmus results from co-contraction of the extraocular muscles on attempted upgaze; the co-contraction of all extraocular muscles causes the globe to retract into the orbit. Dorsal midbrain syndrome also includes lid retraction, upgaze deficit, pupillary light–near dissociation, and increased square-wave jerks. Ptosis, opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome, and ocular flutter are not components of dorsal midbrain syndrome.

pool.q: What disease-modifying medication used for treating multiple sclerosis is most likely to cause flulike symptoms?
pool.rationale:
Interferon therapy is a common treatment for multiple sclerosis. Interferon treatment, such as interferon-beta1b, can often cause flulike symptoms, liver enzyme changes, bone marrow suppression, and thyroid dysfunction. Cystoid macular edema is a side effect of fingolimod, which is a different class of disease-modifying medication for multiple sclerosis. Natalizumab, which is a humanized monoclonal antibody against the cell adhesion molecule α4-integrin, has been associated with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, especially in patients who have previously been exposed to John Cunningham (JC) virus, as well as nausea, infection, and liver dysfunction. Glatiramer acetate causes skin irritation, skin lipoatrophy, and panic attack–like events.

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: A 42-year-old woman had sudden onset of severe right eye redness, mild pain, limited motility, and diplopia. She has normal visual acuity, 7 mm proptosis OD, and intraocular pressure (IOP) 33 mm Hg OD, 12 mm Hg OS. She reports a noise in her right ear. What is the most likely cause of her condition?
pool.rationale:
Abnormal connections between the cavernous sinus and the carotid artery or its branches introduce high arterial pressure into the normally low-pressure venous circulation of the cavernous sinus. These connections can be either high flow or low flow.
The question stem describes signs and symptoms consistent with a direct, high-flow, carotid cavernous fistula, which most commonly occurs after severe head trauma. With acceleration/deceleration injuries, such as head trauma in motor vehicle accidents, the cavernous carotid artery is susceptible to shear forces that may produce a rent in the arterial wall. Pulsatile tinnitus results from arterial flow out of the cavernous sinus and into the inferior petrosal sinus.
Skull base tumors may encase the cavernous carotid but do not cause fistulae to form.
Hypertension, especially in older women, is associated with development of indirect (dural) arteriovenous fistulae with low flow and milder symptoms with insidious onset.
Demyelinating disease does not cause fistula formation.

pool.q: What is the most appropriate next step in managing a new diagnosis of pupil-involving, isolated, complete third cranial nerve palsy?

options.b: computed tomography (CT) with contrast of the orbits
options.d: contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)

pool.rationale:
Third cranial nerve palsies with pupillary involvement must be assumed to be secondary to an aneurysm until proved otherwise. Emergent cerebrovascular imaging (eg, catheter angiography, MRA, or computed tomography angiography [CTA]), depending on clinical scenario and neuroradiologic consultation, should be undertaken.
Careful observation, rather than neuroimaging, may be appropriate when there is an acute, isolated, pupil-sparing, but otherwise complete third nerve palsy in a patient over 50 years of age with appropriate vascular risk factors but without a history of cancer. Complete pupil-sparing third nerve palsies in this setting are almost always due to microvascular ischemia and improve over 3 months. In contrast, some proportion of partial third nerve palsies with normal pupillary function are related to compressive lesions and may later progress to involve the pupil, warranting imaging.
CT with contrast of the orbits is the appropriate next step when a patient presents with an orbital fracture or for compressive orbital lesion detection when MRI is contraindicated, but it can miss an intracranial aneurysm unless paired with CTA.
Carotid doppler ultrasonography is an appropriate next step in the workup of transient unilateral vision loss in order to detect the source of intra-arterial emboli, unrelated to the third nerve palsy in the question.

pool.q: An 85-year-old woman presents with binocular horizontal diplopia at distance. She does not have diplopia with reading. She says that she started wearing glasses in her 40s. Examination demonstrates deep superior sulci, high lid creases, and bilateral ptosis. She has a 10-prism-diopter esotropia at distance, which is comitant. She has mild upgaze limitation with both eyes. What is the most likely cause for her symptoms?
pool.rationale:
Sagging eye syndrome presents in older patients with a mild- to moderate-angle esotropia at distance (ie, divergence insufficiency). Lateral gaze is full, but there can be limitation of supraduction. In sagging eye syndrome, the lateral rectus-superior rectus band degenerates, with inferior displacement of the lateral rectus muscle, along with prolapse of connective tissue superotemporally. In addition, patients often experience degenerative changes causing deep superior sulci, high lid creases, and ptosis resulting from levator aponeurosis dehiscence. 
Myasthenia is less likely because her misalignment is comitant. Heavy eye syndrome can present with progressive esotropia and hypotropia; however, this condition occurs in patients with high myopia. Bilateral sixth-nerve palsies would produce bilateral abduction deficits, and the esotropia would be worse in both right and left gazes.

pool.q: A patient with new onset diplopia has generalized limitation of left eye movement, 3 mm left ptosis, and inferior orbital pain. Visual acuity is normal with no relative afferent pupillary defect, no proptosis, and a normal fundus exam OU. What is the most likely location for the causative lesion?
pool.rationale:
Unilateral painful ophthalmoparesis without a change in visual function or orbital signs such as proptosis is most likely to occur from a cavernous sinus process. Malignancy, inflammation, and thrombosis all can cause multiple cranial neuropathies and pain.
An orbital apex lesion should affect the optic nerve as well and cause vision loss and/or a relative afferent pupillary defect. Dorsal midbrain lesions cause a Parinaud syndrome with upgaze paresis and eyelid retraction bilaterally; this is not a painful condition. Thalamic disease can cause pain and esotropia but not ophthalmoparesis.
