pool.q: For what condition is optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF) indicated?

options.a: Terson syndrome with disc hemorrhage and vitreous hemorrhage
options.b: central retinal vein occlusion with panretinal hemorrhage and macular edema
options.c: sinus thrombosis with increased intracranial pressure, optic disc edema, and visual loss
options.d: traumatic optic neuropathy without disc edema but with profound visual loss

pool.rationale:
In the presence of substantial loss of vision without prominent headache, ONSF may represent the preferred surgical option because it directly protects the optic nerve. However, ONSF carries a 10% to 15% complication rate, including a 1% to 2% risk of vision loss from optic nerve injury, central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), or central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). It does not lower intracranial pressure (ICP) and thus often does not treat headache. A reduction of papilledema in the contralateral eye can occur, but bilateral ONSF may be required. The long-term success rate of ONSF remains unclear. Repeat ONSF may be performed but is technically more difficult because of scarring.
Central retinal vein occlusion with panretinal hemorrhage and macular edema would not be treated with ONSF. Terson syndrome is associated with intraocular hemorrhage associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage. There is no role for ONSF in this setting. Similarly, optic neuropathy from trauma does not improve with ONSF; however, it may improve with orbital decompression of the optic canal in certain cases.

pool.q: The stellate pattern of exudation present in neuroretinitis is a result of fluid deposition and subsequent resorption in what retinal layer?
pool.rationale: The characteristic feature of neuroretinitis is a stellate or "star" pattern of exudates in the macula. This pattern is a result of diffuse optic nerve head edema that spreads through the outer plexiform layer into the macula along the papillomacular bundle around the fovea. Fluid resorption leaves behind lipid precipitates in the characteristic star pattern.

pool.q: A 75-year-old man reports that the vision in his right eye dims out whenever he goes outside into bright light and that his vision slowly improves once he goes back indoors. On examination, the ophthalmologist notices that the central retinal artery "flashes" when gentle pressure is applied to the globe. What diagnostic test should be ordered?

options.a: computed tomography (CT) scan looking for a compressive lesion on the right optic nerve
options.b: carotid angiography (CTA) or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) to look for carotid occlusion on the right
options.c: automated perimetry and diurnal intraocular pressure measurements
options.d: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan looking for enlarged extraocular muscles on the right side

pool.rationale:
Ocular ischemic syndrome is characterized by a hypotensive, ischemic retinopathy with low retinal artery pressure, poor perfusion, and midperipheral retinopathy. Ocular ischemic syndrome can cause transient or persistent blurred vision or transient visual loss upon exposure to bright light. Gentle pressure collapsing the central retinal artery indicates that the perfusion to the central retinal artery is compromised. A CTA or MRA is indicated to look for carotid occlusion ipsilateral to the symptoms.
Compression of the optic nerve typically causes a gradual painless decrease in vision. Enlarged extraocular muscles could cause diplopia or compressive optic neuropathy. Automated perimetry and diurnal intraocular pressure measurements would be indicated if one suspected glaucoma.

pool.q: Following a brainstem stroke, a 68-year-old woman developed diplopia. On examination, the right pupil is larger than the left and is poorly reactive to both direct and consensual stimulus. Both eyes cannot elevate above the horizontal midline. The left eye otherwise moves normally, whereas the right eye can only abduct. Given this clinical presentation, what additional eyelid findings might be expected?

options.a: left upper-eyelid ptosis and lower-eyelid elevation
options.b: bilateral upper-eyelid ptosis and poor levator function
options.c: right upper-eyelid ptosis with fatigability on sustained effort
options.d: bilateral rhythmic eyelid movements with attempted convergence

pool.rationale:
This patient is showing signs of a complete right 3rd nerve palsy and elevation deficit on the left. The symptoms occurred after a brainstem stroke. The bilateral elevation deficit indicates that the stroke involved the right third nerve nucleus within the midbrain.
The third nerve nucleus is a nuclear complex that contains subnuclei for 4 extraocular muscles (superior, inferior, and medial recti, and inferior oblique), a single subnucleus for the levator palpebrae muscles (central caudal nucleus), and paired subnuclei for the pupillary constrictor muscles (Edinger-Westphal nuclei). Because the single central caudal nucleus controls both levator palpebrae muscles, and the superior rectus fascicles decussate just after emerging from their subnuclei, lesions of the third nerve nuclear complex can cause bilateral ptosis and bilaterally affect the superior rectus muscles.
Left upper-eyelid ptosis and lower-eyelid elevation with a smaller pupil is suggestive of Horner syndrome; however, this overall clinical presentation is not consistent with oculosympathetic paresis. Right upper-eyelid ptosis with fatigability suggests myasthenia. However, myasthenia would not cause anisocoria. Bilateral rhythmic eyelid movements with attempted convergence are seen with dorsal midbrain syndrome. Dorsal midbrain syndrome can cause elevation deficits but would also not cause anisocoria.

pool.q: A 19-year-old woman has new headaches and transient visual obscurations. She has severe acne and uses a topical medication prescribed by her dermatologist. She weighs 110 pounds and is 5 feet, 2 inches tall. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU with normal color vision. Static perimetry shows blind spot enlargement bilaterally, and ductions are full. Her anterior segments are normal. What optic disc finding might you expect to see on fundoscopy?
pool.rationale:
Bilateral optic disc swelling is observed in papilledema from increased intracranial pressure. Use of topical anti-acne medication (including tetracyclines like minocycline, as well as retinoic acid) is associated with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), as in this case.
Normal disc appearance is incorrect because the patient's history and visual field findings are consistent with papilledema.
Optic nerve pallor is incorrect because there is no indication of optic neuropathy, suggested by visual field with only blind spot enlargement, normal color vision, and normal visual acuity.
Mild hyperemia with telangiectatic vasculature is characteristic of pseudopapilledema from Leber hereditary optic neuropathy in the acute stage, or possibly consistent with diabetic papillitis. Neither diagnosis is indicated in this prompt, which describes a young female with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure.

pool.q: What is the cause of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) in patients with hemianopic vision loss from an optic tract lesion?

options.a: improper retinal illumination during the swinging flashlight test
options.b: compression of the ipsilateral third cranial nerve
options.c: asymmetric decussation of the pupillary fibers at the chiasm
options.d: extension of the responsible lesion to the optic nerve

pool.rationale:
Anterior optic tract lesions from tumor compression or stroke create a homonymous hemianopia and may be accompanied by a RAPD contralateral to the lesion (ie, on the same side as the hemianopia). The RAPD occurs because the lesion affects more fibers from the contralateral optic nerve. About 53% of fibers from each optic nerve cross at the chiasm, and this asymmetry is enough to cause a mild RAPD with a tract lesion.
Although improper technique can lead the examiner to a false conclusion regarding the presence or absence of an RAPD, that is not the cause here.
Optic nerve involvement can actually negate the RAPD, because the contralateral RAPD would be balanced out by an ipsilateral optic neuropathy. CN III compression gives an efferent, not an afferent, pupillary defect.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What would be expected with a left cranial III nerve nucleus lesion?

options.a: bilateral ptosis, left adduction and depression deficit, right elevation deficit
options.b: left ptosis, adduction, and depression deficit, right depression deficit
options.c: bilateral ptosis, left elevation and adduction deficit, right depression deficit
options.d: left ptosis, elevation, adduction, and depression deficit

pool.rationale: The CN III is a nuclear complex that contains subnuclei for 4 extraocular muscles (superior, inferior, medial recti, and inferior oblique), a single subnucleus (central caudal nucleus) for the levator palpebrae muscles, and paired subnuclei (Edinger-Westphal nuclei) for the pupillary constrictor muscles. Because the single central caudal nucleus controls both levator palpebrae superioris muscles, and the superior rectus fascicles decussate just after emerging from their subnuclei, lesions of the CN III nuclear complex either affect or spare both upper eyelids and may affect the contralateral superior rectus muscle (not ipsilateral rectus muscle). Therefore, a left CN III nuclear lesion would be expected to cause bilateral ptosis, right elevation deficit, and left adduction and depression deficits. Because the superior rectus fibers pass adjacent to the contralateral superior rectus subnuclei, bilateral elevation deficits can also be seen with CN III nuclear lesions.

pool.q: A 21-year-old woman develops asymptomatic, hyperemic disc edema in the right eye with telangiectatic changes. Her visual acuity is 20/20, and she has a trace relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). What is most likely responsible for this examination finding?

options.a: nocturnal hypotension with crowded optic disc

pool.rationale:
Of the answer choices provided, diabetic papillopathy is most likely in this younger woman with asymptomatic, unilateral, painless, hyperemic optic disc edema. Diabetic papillopathy can occur in type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Patients may have no symptoms or have nonspecific symptoms of “blurred vision” or “distortion” without pain. The optic nerve reveals hyperemic edema, but 50% of patients show marked dilation of the disc surface microvasculature that appears similar to neovascularization of the disc. Often, but not always, diabetic retinopathy findings such as retinal microaneurysms or dot-blot hemorrhages are present. Treatment is directed at correcting the underlying hyperglycemia.
Nocturnal hypotension in a patient with a crowded optic disc is associated with nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). NAION occurs most frequently in middle-aged hypertensive patients on beta-blockers. It causes acute vision loss, especially upon waking and in the lower half of the visual field. It is rare in patients younger than 40 years old.
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is a mitochondrial myopathy, inherited through the female bloodline and phenotypically present primarily in male family members. It causes acute or subacute central vision loss in one, then both eyes. It is usually found in symptomatic males in their second and third decades.
Optic nerve glioma is a disease primarily of children, presenting as chronic, progressive optic nerve pallor and proptosis, not optic disc edema.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 51-year-old French-Canadian woman presents with constant ptosis, poor levator function, and difficulty swallowing. What inheritance pattern is most likely to be found for her condition?
pool.rationale: The constellation of findings in this woman supports the diagnosis of oculopharyngeal dystrophy. Oculopharyngeal dystrophy (also termed "oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy") is characterized by late-onset (usually after the age of 45 years) ptosis, swallowing difficulty, and a positive family history, with involvement of 2 or more generations. Oculopharyngeal dystrophy is inherited in either an autosomal dominant or an autosomal recessive manner. Sporadic inheritance is not characteristic of oculopharyngeal dystrophy, and X-linked mitochondrial patterns of transmission do not occur.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with lid retraction of both upper lids, bilateral proptosis, and limited abduction of both eyes. What finding on physical examination would confirm medial rectus muscle restriction?
pool.rationale:
The patient presents with classic signs of thyroid eye disease, which has a predilection toward causing inferior rectus and medial rectus enlargement and restrictive strabismus. Restrictive strabismus can be confirmed with the forced duction test. A restrictive process produces a mechanical limitation of the range of eye movements that can often be felt by an examiner when forceps or a cotton swab is used to advance the limited eye movement.
Paretic conditions reduce the saccadic velocity, whereas restrictive conditions do not. Esotropia would be expected for a limitation of abduction of both eyes, but would not differentiate between a paralytic or restrictive process. A comitant misalignment is typically seen in patients with congenital or early-onset strabismus.

pool.q: What supranuclear ocular motor system is responsible for maintaining an image on the fovea during brief head movements?
pool.rationale: The vestibular-ocular system holds the image of an object on the fovea during brief head movement. The optokinetic system holds the image of an object on the fovea during sustained head movement. The ocular fixation system holds the image of a stationary object on the fovea when there is no head movement. The vergence system enables the eyes to move in opposite directions so that the image of an object remains on the fovea of both the right and left eyes for near and distance viewing with normal ocular alignment.

pool.q: What pharmacologic test result would confirm a third-order Horner syndrome?

options.a: lack of pupillary dilation with topical cocaine in the affected eye
options.b: pupillary dilation with hydroxyamphetamine drop in the affected eye
options.c: lack of pupillary dilation with hydroxyamphetamine drop in the affected eye
options.d: pupillary dilation with topical cocaine in the affected eye

pool.rationale:
Horner syndrome is an ocular sympathetic paresis caused by a disruption of the superior cervical sympathetic chain. The interruption can be classified as first-, second-, or third- order neuron injury depending on the level of the injury.
Horner syndrome can be diagnosed pharmacologically with topical cocaine or apraclonidine. Topical cocaine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine released in the synaptic clefts leading to pupillary dilation in an unaffected eye. However, in Horner syndrome, because there is no norepinephrine in the synaptic clefts, cocaine has no effect, and the miotic pupil does not dilate. Of note, apraclonidine can also confirm a Horner syndrome by reversal of anisocoria.
Similarly, a hydroxyamphetamine eyedrop dilates normal pupils by releasing catecholamines from the motor end plate. Dilation occurs if the third-order neuron is intact; no dilation occurs if the third-order neuron is involved. Therefore, no pupillary dilation with a hydroxyamphetamine drop confirms a third-order Horner syndrome. 
First-order neuron lesions arise from the hypothalamus to the spinal cord (often caused by vascular lesions or tumors); second-order neuron lesions arise from the spinal cord to superior cervical ganglion (often caused by trauma or tumors affecting the cervicothoracic spinal cord); and third-order neuron lesions arise from the superior cervical ganglion along the internal carotid artery to tarsal muscles and the pupillary dilator muscle (often caused by tumors, inflammatory lesions, trauma, or ischemia).
In summary, topical cocaine and apraclonidine can confirm a Horner syndrome, whereas hydroxyamphetamine can distinguish a 3rd order from a first- or second-order Horner syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What disease is characterized by an impaired ability to repair sunlight-induced damage to DNA and may manifest signs of keratoconjunctivitis sicca and blepharospasm?
pool.rationale:
Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by an impaired ability to repair sunlight-induced damage to DNA. On exposed skin, patients develop hyperpigmentation, atrophy, actinic keratosis, and telangiectasia. Cutaneous neoplasms are common later in life. Ocular changes include keratoconjunctivitis sicca, blepharospasm, conjunctival telangiectasia and hyperpigmentation, symblepharon, eyelid atrophy and scarring, trichiasis, and ocular neoplasms (11% of patients, more common at the limbus).
Ichthyosis (AD) is a desquamating skin condition that is not responsive to corticosteroid treatment. It is known to have primary corneal opacities, band keratopathy, and cornea vascularization. The eyelids are frequently involved with scaling and cicatricial ectropion. Keratoconjunctivitis sicca may be present in these patients but it is not due to abnormal DNA repair.
Meige syndrome is a combination of essential blepharospasm with facial grimacing. This condition is not caused by abnormal DNA repair. The etiology of Meige syndrome is unknown. For these patients, consider checking a computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan to rule out posterior fossa lesions. Patients with Meige syndrome can be treated with botulinum toxin injections to the affected area or with systemic medications (tetrabenazine, lithium, carbidopa, clonazepam). Dry eye syndrome (DES) has been known to cause blepharospasm.
Sjögren syndrome is defined as keratoconjunctivitis sicca, xerostomia (decreased parotid flow rate), lymphocytic infiltration in the salivary glands on biopsy, and laboratory evidence of systemic autoimmune disease (positive ANA, RF, SS-A, or SS-B). Sjögren syndrome is not associated with abnormal DNA repair.

pool.q: A 45-year-old immunocompromised patient developed a left retrobulbar optic neuropathy, diplopia, and headache. He was found to have a lesion in the sphenoid sinus extending to the left orbital apex. Biopsy showed organisms with septate hyphae. What organism is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?
pool.rationale:
Aspergillus

Biopsy showed septate hyphae, which is consistent with Aspergillus. Aspergillomas, or fungus balls, can involve the sinuses and can extend to the optic canal or cavernous sinus, leading to optic neuropathy and diplopia. Mucormycosis, Candida, and Streptococcus pneumoniae would not show septate hyphae on culture.

pool.q: A 45-year-old man presents with suspected nonorganic vision loss after a motor vehicle accident. His attorney has asked for a visual evoked potential (VEP) test to assess optic nerve function. How will the VEP results be helpful in this case?

options.a: A normal VEP confirms intact afferent visual pathways, and an abnormal VEP proves pathology.
options.b: A normal VEP confirms intact afferent visual pathways, but an abnormal VEP is nonspecific and does not prove pathology.
options.c: A prolonged P100 amplitude is specific for functional visual loss.
options.d: A prolonged P100 latency is specific for functional visual loss.

pool.rationale:
Visual-evoked potential (VEP) testing is an objective method to determine the integrity of the afferent visual pathway from the retina to the occipital cortex. Normal responses confirm intact visual pathways. Nevertheless, numerous factors may produce abnormal VEP waveforms in the absence of visual pathway damage, including uncorrected refractive error, media opacity, amblyopia, fatigue, and inattention (intended or unintended). VEP accuracy depends on patient cooperation and several other factors.
P100 latency is likely to be markedly delayed in demyelination of the optic nerve. Reduction in P100 amplitude may occur secondary to ischemic, compressive, or toxic optic nerve damage and is, therefore, not specific to a particular cause.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 55-year-old man has diplopia at distance with esotropia worse on left gaze. What office test is most helpful in differentiating a restrictive from a paralytic strabismus as the cause of the double vision?
pool.rationale:
A restrictive process produces a mechanical limitation of the range of eye movements that can often be felt by the examiner when forceps or a cotton swab is used to advance the limited eye movements. To perform a forced duction test, topical proparacaine drops are applied to the eye and held over the limbal region with a cotton tip for 1 to 2 minutes. Then the conjunctiva at the limbus is grasped with toothed forceps, and the globe is passively rotated in the direction of limited abduction to assess for restriction of eye movement. A positive forced duction test results when there is restriction to passive eye movement.
Alternate cover testing, rather than cover/uncover, will unmask any phoria but will not inform the examiner about muscle function. Monocular occlusion is useful when the examiner suspects strabismus in a patient with no manifest deviation, as it breaks fusion and can unmask a latent strabismus. Orbital cooling has been suggested in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis but cannot distinguish other paretic causes (such as 6th nerve palsy) from a restrictive process.

pool.q: What brainstem structure is responsible for generating horizontal saccades?

options.d: rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus

pool.rationale: The excitatory burst neurons for generating horizontal saccades are located in the paramedian pontine reticular formation. The medial longitudinal fasciculus contains neurons that project from the CN VI nucleus to the contralateral CN III nucleus and mediates horizontal yoke muscle movement. The rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal are located in the midbrain and are involved in the generation of torsional and vertical saccades.

pool.q: A patient has transient monocular vision loss that is associated with eye pain. The pain improves when the patient lies down. What is the most likely cause?

options.b: vasculitis due to giant cell arteritis

pool.rationale: Ocular hypoperfusion due to carotid occlusive disease (ocular ischemic syndrome) can cause transient monocular vision loss, typically in setting of bright light exposure. Recurrent eye pain that improves when the patient is lying down is highly suggestive of ocular ischemic syndrome. The examination may demonstrate midperipheral dot-blot hemorrhages and dilated veins due to low central retinal artery pressure. Patients may also develop episcleral injection and aqueous flare due to ischemic uveitis. Neovascularization of the angle or of the iris is common, although intraocular pressure (IOP) can be high, normal, or low. Low or normal intraocular pressure can result from ciliary body hypoperfusion.

pool.q: A 63-year-old man undergoes a prolonged spine surgery in the prone position and awakens with light perception vision in both eyes. What is the most likely appearance of the optic nerves?
pool.rationale: Vision loss upon awakening from spine surgery is classically posterior ischemic optic neuropathy (PION) affecting the optic nerve. Vision loss in perioperative PION is more commonly bilateral and profound. The appearance of the optic nerve initially is normal. Over time, pallor develops. Patients can have anterior ischemic optic neuropathy following surgery and present initially with optic disc edema, but PION is the classic presentation of vision loss following spine surgery and prolonged prone position. Cupping is seen in glaucoma and would not present this acutely.

pool.q: What is the most helpful neuroimaging modality in managing a 35-year-old female patient's first episode of acute, unilateral optic neuritis?

options.b: orbital MRI with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging
options.c: orbital magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with T1 post-contrast fat-saturation

pool.rationale:
Optic neuritis is a clinical diagnosis based on historical and examination findings. Orbital MRI with T1 post-contrast fat-saturation, especially coronal and axial views, can confirm the optic nerve enhancement consistent with the diagnosis. However, of the choices provided, the correct answer is brain MRI with FLAIR imaging, because in managing this patient, the most important factor is determining her multiple sclerosis (MS) risk. Risk of MS is directly related to the presence of concomitant brain MRI demyelinating lesions, best seen on FLAIR and often periventricular.
Orbital MRI with FLAIR may show optic nerve diameter asymmetry and subtle enhancement but is of less prognostic value and is less helpful without fat saturation. Orbital CT with contrast is excellent in screening for large mass lesions of the orbit but has limited value with assessing inflammatory soft tissue disease and would not be prognostically helpful in this scenario.

pool.q: A patient has slowly progressive left eye vision and visual field loss from an optic nerve sheath meningioma (ONSM). What treatment is most effective in preventing further visual loss?
pool.rationale:
Patients with vision loss from ONSM should be offered fractionated stereotactic radiation therapy, as this therapy has been shown to preserve or even improve visual function in up to 95% of patients.
Surgical excision carries a high risk of disrupting the blood supply to the nerve and should not be perfomed. Although steroids may temporarily improve optic nerve swelling (if present), they have no long-term effect. No effective chemotherapy for meningioma exists.

pool.q: What cancer is most commonly associated with cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR)?
pool.rationale:
CAR is also known as a paraneoplastic autoimmune retinopathy (pAIR). Although pAIRs have been described with numerous cancers, small-cell lung carcinoma is the most frequent cause of these disorders. Autoimmune retinopathy can be suspected when symptoms of nyctalopia and photopsias are elicited. Signs include visual field constriction, outer retinal disruption on optical coherence tomography, abnormalities on fundus autofluorescence, and abnormalities on electrophysiologic testing. A neoplastic etiology should be sought out; this typically includes a physical examination, laboratory testing, and radiographic imaging (computed tomography [CT], magnetic resonance imaging [MRI], or positron emission tomography [PET] scan).
Melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR), another type of pAIR, shares some features with CAR, but is given its own name (MAR) and is not referred to as CAR. One feature that seems to differentiate MAR from CAR is that color vision and central vision are typically preserved in MAR.
Metastatic adenocarcinoma (if it metastasized to the eye) would be expected to present as a choroidal mass. Colon cancer can produce pAIR, but small-cell lung cancer is more common. The ocular manifestation of central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma is as primary intraocular lymphoma (now increasingly referred to as primary vitreoretinal lymphoma). Paraneoplastic AIR has not been described in primary CNS or intraocular lymphomas.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What condition commonly leads to congenital Horner syndrome?
pool.rationale: Congenital Horner syndrome is most commonly caused by birth trauma to the brachial plexus. If there is no history of trauma, then the patient should have a workup for congenital tumors such as neuroblastoma.

pool.q: When does radiation optic neuropathy typically occur after radiation therapy?
pool.rationale: Radiation optic neuropathy is a complication that occurs after radiation that involves the optic nerves. This typically occurs months (average 18 months) after radiation treatment and produces subacute optic neuropathy. Radiation optic neuropathy is in part dose-related; it is more likely to occur with higher doses (typically > 5000 cGy). MRI typically shows enhancement of the optic nerves.

pool.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with the sudden onset of left-sided eye pain accompanied by ipsilateral ptosis, impaired ocular motility–sparing abduction, and a fixed and dilated (8 mm) pupil. What are head imaging studies most likely to show?
pool.rationale:
The possibility of an aneurysm at the origin of the posterior communicating artery from the internal carotid artery must be urgently evaluated in a patient presenting with a new-onset painful pupil-involving third cranial nerve palsy. Saccular (“berry”) aneurysms are the most common cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), and the origin of the posterior communicating artery is a frequently involved site. Intracerebral hemorrhage, which is most commonly due to hypertension, can present with focal neurologic symptoms but a pupil-sparing third cranial nerve palsy would be atypical.
Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) can cause intracerebral hemorrhage as well as SAH. When associated with SAH, AVMs may manifest with focal seizures, progressive worsening of focal neurologic signs, and recurrent unilateral migraine-like headache. Intraventricular hemorrhage usually occurs as a secondary phenomenon in patients with an intracerebral or subarachnoid hemorrhage. It typically manifests with sudden-onset headache, nausea, vomiting, and varying degrees of impaired consciousness. Microvascular ischemia to the third cranial nerve can also cause sudden-onset pain, ptosis, and partial ophthalmoplegia, but pupil involvement is generally mild (less than 1 mm of anisocoria).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Following a motor vehicle accident 2 days ago, a 25-year-old woman reports painful sudden vision loss in her right eye. She has not lost consciousness and had no head or facial trauma. Visual acuity is light perception OD, 20/20 OS with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Anterior and posterior segment examination is normal. She reports diplopia viewing the 20/40 line with 4 PD base down OS. What is the most appropriate action in managing this patient?

options.a: urgent computed tomography (CT) orbits with fine cuts through the optic canals
options.b: serologic testing for syphilis and Lyme disease
options.d: intravenous methylprednisolone 1 gram daily for 3 days

pool.rationale:
This scenario describes nonphysiologic vision loss occurring after a motor vehicle accident. The key findings supporting this diagnosis are mechanism of injury not suggestive of severity of vision loss, as well as examination inconsistencies such as light perception (LP) vision OD without relative afferent pupillary defect. In addition, diplopia while testing the 20/40 line with mild induced prism over 1 eye demonstrates that her vision is much better than LP. In this setting, reassurance with close follow-up is appropriate.
Serologic testing for syphilis and Lyme disease, intravenous methylprednisolone, and/or urgent CT are not indicated in this case, because there was a normal eye examination with no demonstrable optic neuropathy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Three weeks ago, a 42-year-old woman had clipping of a left posterior communicating aneurysm. Prior to surgery, she had no diplopia but noted constant diplopia immediately after the surgery. Examination showed a pupil-involving third nerve palsy. Levator function is partially spared. What would be the preferred acute management?
pool.rationale: This patient developed a third nerve palsy from the clipping of the left posterior communicating aneurysm, which is a common complication of this surgery. Monocular occlusion is the preferred treatment in the acute setting for patients with symptomatic diplopia. Some patients get some spontaneous recovery and therefore immediate strabismus surgery is not recommended. Because of the incomitant nature and expected improvement in some cases, ground-in-prisms are not recommended. Pencil pushups are a treatment option for convergence insufficiency.

pool.q: A patient presents with optic nerve head (ONH) swelling and delayed choroidal filling on fluorescein angiography. What condition do they most likely have?
pool.rationale: Fluoroscein angiography might demonstrate delayed or absent choroidal filling in a patient with giant cell arteritis. This can be either with or without ONH edema. Other causes of optic-nerve swelling might show ONH leakage on angiography, but will not show delayed choroidal filling.

pool.q: In benign essential blepharospasm, where in the central nervous system is the seventh nerve hyperactivity thought to originate?
pool.rationale: Functional neuroimaging suggests that benign essential blepharospasm occurs due to dysfunction of the basal ganglia. Hemifacial spasm occurs due to compression of the facial root in the cerebellopontine angle. Facial myokymia occurs due to intramedullary disease of the pons at the facial nucleus or fascicle.

pool.q: A 38-year-old man has periodic right-sided headache with right eye redness and tearing. The pain occasionally wakes him from sleep. What additional right eye/orbital sign is most likely to be associated with his headache events?
pool.rationale: Unilateral headache with eye redness and tearing characterizes trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias, which include cluster headache, sudden unilateral neuralgiform headache with conjunctival redness and tearing (SUNCT), hemicrania continua, and others. Autonomic dysfunction and Horner syndrome-like findings may accompany the headache pain, and 1 mm to 2 mm eyelid ptosis may be seen. The pupil may be miotic, not dilated (as may occur with migraine headache), and intraocular inflammation and/or disc swelling are not caused by these headaches.
