pool.q: A 10-year-old boy with a history of neurofibromatosis type 1 presented with no light perception (NLP) vision, prominent and disfiguring proptosis, and corneal scarring OD. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve approaching the chiasm. What is the most likely preferred management of this lesion?
pool.rationale:
Optic pathway gliomas (OPG) in children, including optic gliomas confined to the optic nerve body itself, are almost always benign astrocytomas whose natural history is stable without significant progression over time. Some may even show spontaneous regression. Thus, there is no universally accepted management of OPG, but indications for treatment depend on clinical progression by vision loss, loss of visual quality of life, or extension of the lesion into the optic chiasm (rare). Radiation or chemotherapy treatment depends on age and association with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Surgical treatment may be entertained in cases of severe vision loss, with the purpose of reducing disfiguring proptosis and extension into the chiasm.
In this case, careful observation is not preferred, because the tumor is approaching the chiasm, there is no visual potential in the affected eye, and the patient has disfiguring proptosis. Radiation is not preferred in this case, due to significant long-term side effects with NF1, although it can be an option in patients over 5 years old with progressive optic nerve glioma. Chemotherapy with carboplatin and vincristine is an emerging first-line treatment, but surgical resection is probably preferred in this case due to the need to better address the disfiguring proptosis and corneal scarring.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the biggest risk factor for the formation of a direct carotid-cavernous fistula?
pool.rationale:
Abnormal connections between the cavernous sinus and the carotid artery or its branches introduce the high pressure of the arterial system into the normally low-pressure venous system, which may reverse flow in the superior ophthalmic vein and cause orbital congestion. Direct connections between the internal carotid artery and the cavernous sinus typically produce a high-flow fistula and usually occur after head trauma.
Low flow, indirect or "dural' cavernous fistulas occur when small meningeal arterial branches communicate with venous drainage. Indirect fistulas form most often as a degenerative process in older women with systemic hypertension and atherosclerosis.
Diabetes and neurofibromatosis are not risk factors for carotid-cavernous fistula formation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. He is unconscious. The left pupil is larger than the right. What finding on his limited eye examination suggests trauma to the left optic nerve?

options.a: tonic right pupil after swinging a flashlight over the right pupil
options.b: tonic left pupil after swinging a flashlight over the left pupil
options.c: dilation of the right pupil after swinging a flashlight over the left pupil
options.d: constriction of the left pupil after swinging a flashlight over the left pupil

pool.rationale:
Eye examination is challenging in the unconscious patient due to inability to obtain subjective information such as vision, color, and visual field testing. Dilated fundus examination may initially be normal. However, the assessment of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), heralded by an abnormal swinging-flashlight test, raises suspicion of traumatic optic neuropathy.
In this patient with anisocoria, RAPD can be detected only by reverse testing, as the dilated left pupil is more suggestive of traumatic mydriasis than optic neuropathy. Initial constriction of the healthy right eye to light over the right pupil, followed by dilation or poor constriction of the right eye to light over the left pupil, confirms an RAPD by reverse testing and suggests traumatic optic neuropathy in this context.
Tonic left pupil after swinging a flashlight over the left pupil is not the correct answer, because this observation cannot confirm an RAPD in the setting of baseline mydriasis.
Tonic right pupil after swinging a flashlight over the right pupil is not the correct answer, because this observation does not give information about the left eye.
Constriction of the left pupil after swinging a flashlight over the left pupil is not the correct answer, because this observation would suggest intact optic nerve function of the left eye.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 73-year-old woman reports several episodes of transient monocular vision loss over the past 2 weeks. Visual acuity is normal. The fundus examination is unremarkable. Fluorescein angiography shows delayed early perfusion and patchy choroidal filling in both eyes. Perimetry is normal. What is the next step in evaluating or managing this patient's condition?

options.a: catheter angiography with left carotid stenting
options.d: intravitreal injection of an anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agent

pool.rationale:
The fluorescein angiogram in this case confirms poor choroidal circulation. The choroid is supplied primarily from branches of the ophthalmic artery, which in this age group is a main target of giant cell arteritis (GCA). Since the concern for GCA is raised, even in the absence of arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient is to initiate immediate treatment with a high-dose steroid and obtain laboratory results regarding inflammation, then do a temporal artery biopsy to determine the pathologic diagnosis.
Catheter angiography with left carotid stenting is incorrect, because this patient's examination did not include the mid-peripheral dot-blot hemorrhages or anterior segment findings of ocular ischemic syndrome due to atherosclerotic occlusion of the carotid and ophthalmic artery, but this is within the differential diagnosis and carotid vascular evaluation may be necessary in the setting of negative temporal artery biopsy. Intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF therapy is not correct, because there are no signs of neovascularization mentioned on examination. Finally, multifocal electroretinography is unnecessary, because the choroidal circulation has already been defined as the source of her symptoms and would not contribute to the initial diagnostic workup.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A thin 57-year-old man complains of horizontal diplopia for the past week and a frontal headache for the past month that are worse upon awakening. On examination, he has bilateral optic disc edema. Visual fields are full, except for a blind spot enlargement. Magnetic resonance images (MRIs) of the brain with and without gadolinium reveal slightly small ventricles and posterior globe flattening. Lumbar puncture reveals an opening pressure of 425 mm of water with normal composition. What is the most appropriate patient management?

options.a: magnetic resonance venogram (MRV) of the cerebral venous drainage system
options.b: immediate treatment with optic nerve sheath fenestration (ONSF)
options.d: initiation of a low-sodium weight loss program

pool.rationale:
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) can present with signs and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), similar to that of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), because of decreased venous outflow. It is important to rule out CVST with MRV, especially in patients who do not fit the classic demographic profile of IIH (obese woman of childbearing age). Treatment for CVST includes anticoagulation and systemic workup.
The other answer choices are incorrect because further diagnostic workup is indicated. IIH is a diagnosis of exclusion. Initial treatment of IIH begins with weight loss intervention and/or acetazolamide, an oral agent that decreases cerebrospinal fluid production. A low-sodium weight loss program would not be indicated for CVST. Although acetazolamide may be used in conjunction with anticoagulation for CVST, this answer is incorrect because the patient requires further diagnostic workup. ONSF is an option in patients with severe vision loss from papilledema, but this patient has only mild visual field defects.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 33-year-old man had sudden, complete, painless vision loss in his left eye that lasted 10 to 15 minutes, before remitting completely. On examination, his visual acuity, perimetry, and fundus appearance are normal. The right pupil is 1 mm larger than the left and dilates more quickly in darkness. There is no relative afferent pupillary defect. The left eyelid has 2 mm ptosis. What environmental insult might be elicited on further questioning?

options.b: attempted weight loss through a restrictive diet
options.c: dehydration 3 months ago after completing his first triathlon

pool.rationale:
The patient’s examination result is concerning for a left Horner syndrome, which is characterized clinically by ipsilateral miosis, facial anhidrosis, and ptosis. A Horner syndrome can be caused an internal carotid dissection, which can lead to stroke or amaurotic episodes. Among the options provided, a roller coaster ride could increase the risk of a carotid dissection. The other options would not predispose a patient to a Horner syndrome or carotid dissection.
A long commercial flight could predispose to development of deep venous thrombosis. However, in the absence of a patent foramen ovale, this would not be expected to cause transient monocular vision loss, and it should not lead to a Horner syndrome.
It is possible that dehydration due to prolonged exertion could predispose to hypoperfusion and related ischemia, such as a nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Dehydration would not cause a Horner syndrome.
Restrictive diets can lead to vitamin deficiencies and nutritional optic neuropathy but would not be expected to cause transient monocular vision loss or Horner syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What condition is the most common cause of divergence insufficiency (DI) in an otherwise healthy adult patient?

options.d: connective tissue involution between the superior and lateral rectus muscles

pool.rationale:
DI is an acquired ocular misalignment defined by an esodeviation that is greater at distance than near fixation, without lateral incomitance, and without abduction deficits. This disorder is usually benign and not related to neurologic dysfunction. In older patients, DI often results from involution of the connective tissue band between the superior and lateral rectus muscles, causing inferior displacement of the lateral rectus muscles (ie, sagging eye syndrome). The malpositioned lateral rectus muscles have reduced abduction force, resulting in DI pattern esotropia. Rarely, DI can be caused by neurological disorders such as increased intracranial pressure, midbrain tumors, Miller Fisher syndrome, head trauma, intracranial hypotension, Arnold-Chiari malformation, and cerebellar degeneration (often with other signs of these disorders).
A lesion in the CN VI nucleus results in a gaze palsy.
A lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus results in an internuclear ophthalmoplegia characterized by impaired adduction and an abducting nystagmus during horizontal gaze opposite the side of the lesion.
Enlarged medial rectus muscles that impair abduction are characteristic of thyroid-related orbitopathy.muscles
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the preferred imaging test to evaluate a slowly progressive facial nerve palsy with myokymia?

options.d: PET scan of the periventricular region

pool.rationale: Slowly progressive facial palsies strongly suggest the diagnosis of a brainstem mass. Facial myokymia derives from continuous or undulating contraction of facial muscle fascicles, usually originating from the intramedullary pons. These rippling movements usually begin within a portion of the orbicularis oculi and may spread to involve other facial muscles. In children, a disorder of the pons is most likely a pontine glioma, and in an adult, the condition is most likely to be multiple sclerosis. Although myokymia may rarely be due to Guillain-Barré syndrome, imaging of the brainstem is most important. Neither a PET scan of the periventricular region nor a CT scan of the orbits would be likely to demonstrate pathology related to the facial nerve.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 78-year-old man developed a stroke with mild arm and leg weakness and a right facial nerve palsy. His right eyelids do not close completely. What other aspect of his examination is most important for his risk of corneal ulceration?
pool.rationale:
In patients with facial nerve palsy, the most crucial question is the status of the trigeminal nerve. Patients developing facial nerve palsy from stroke or intracranial surgery are also at risk of developing a trigeminal neuropathy that may eliminate their corneal sensitivity. The combination of an anesthetic cornea and lagophthalmos places these patients at a very high risk of developing corneal exposure and ulceration. Intact corneal sensation is protective for maintaining blink reflex and lacrimation, especially in patients who may lack concomitant upgaze with lid closure (Bell phenomenon). The risk of combined neurotrophic and neuroparalytic keratitis demands an aggressive approach that possibly includes early tarsorrhaphy or gold weight implant.
Although an intact Bell phenomenon may help protect the cornea from exposure in some cases of lagophthalmos, corneal sensation is the most important exam finding to help determine risk of corneal ulceration. Lissamine green stain may highlight devitalized conjunctival epithelial cells, but this is not predictive for ulceration. Conjunctival culture to assess the ocular surface flora is also not predictive of risk of corneal complications.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 67-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presents with progressively worsening diplopia and decreased vision in the left eye. On examination, the left eye shows a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), ptosis on the left, and limited ductions of the left eye in all directions. Also, corneal sensation is diminished in the left eye. Based on this constellation of symptoms, where is the lesion expected?
pool.rationale:
This patient has signs of a left optic neuropathy (left RAPD), affecting at least the left cranial nerves (CNs III, V1, and VI), based on the findings of ptosis, limited ductions in all directions, and decreased corneal sensation. The combination of CN II and ophthalmoplegia localizes to the orbital apex. If CN II is unaffected, the location of the lesion would be expected in the ipsilateral cavernous sinus.
The hallmark of ophthalmoplegia secondary to a lesion of the cavernous sinus is ipsilateral ocular motor nerve dysfunction involving any combination of third, fourth, fifth, and sixth CNs and sympathetic fibers. The offending lesion may extend toward the optic foramen or into the orbital apex, in which case optic nerve function can be compromised. The designation orbital apex syndrome is then applied.
A brain stem lesion can cause various craniopathies, but would not be expected to cause an optic neuropathy.
A cortical lesion would not be expected to cause an optic neuropathy or unilateral ophthalmoplegia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The lacrimal pump system is driven by what nerve?
pool.rationale: The lacrimal pump is driven by the action of the pretarsal orbicular oculi muscle, which is innervated by the facial nerve, or CN VII. CN III is the oculomotor nerve that supplies the medial, superior, and inferior rectus and oblique muscles, as well as the levator muscle. CN V is the trigeminal nerve; it supplies sensory innervation to the face as well as motor innervation to some muscles of mastication. CN VI innervates the abducens nerve.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 32-year-old woman slipped on ice and sustained blunt head trauma. Her workup including a computed tomography (CT) scan, which was negative. Since then, she has experienced horizontal uncrossed diplopia, which is greater in left gaze. It does not vary with the time of day. The vision is 20/20 in each eye. When the right eye fixes, the deviation in the primary position is 20 prism diopters of left esotropia, 10 prism diopters on right gaze, and 30 prism diopters on left gaze. When the left eye fixes, the right esotropia in the primary position is 30 prism diopters, 20 prism diopters in right gaze, and 40 prism diopters in left gaze. What best explains the difference in the measurements dependent on which eye is fixing?

options.a: There is a fracture of the nasal wall of the left orbit.
options.b: A secondary deviation is greater than a primary deviation.
options.c: The patient has developed myasthenia gravis.
options.d: A primary deviation is greater than a secondary deviation.

pool.rationale:
The findings are consistent with a weakness of the left lateral rectus. The amount of innervation to synergist muscles is determined by the fixating eye. The primary deviation is the amount of strabismus present with the normal eye fixating. The secondary deviation is the amount of strabismus with the paretic eye fixating. Since the deviation was greater with the left eye fixating, it was the result of secondary deviation. Increased innervation to the weak left lateral rectus is necessary to allow the paretic eye to move to the point of fixation, which creates the same extra innervation to the yoke right medial rectus. This increases the amount of esotropia measured. A secondary deviation is always greater than primary deviation.
Myasthenia gravis is not likely as there was no fluctuation during the day, and ptosis was not present. A nasal orbital wall fracture could cause decreased abduction, but it was ruled out by the normal CT scan.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what nonocular disorder is nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF), caused by the use of a gadolinium-based contrast agent, most likely to occur?
pool.rationale: NSF is often seen in patients with kidney disease. The risk of NSF increases with lower glomerular filtration rate because the kidneys are primarily responsible for clearing gadolinium contrast. Chronic liver disease is not a significant risk factor for NSF. Heart and lung disease are not associated with NSF.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 57-year-old man reports new-onset anisocoria. His right pupil is 4.5 mm, and his left is 3.0 mm. His right palpebral fissure is 11 mm; his left is 9.5 mm. He has pain that radiates up the left side of his neck to his orbit. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.a: dissection of the left internal carotid artery
options.c: cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) on the left

pool.rationale:
The presence of ipsilateral miosis and ptosis is concerning for Horner syndrome, which is caused by a lesion at any point along the oculosympathetic pathway. A painful Horner syndrome is most commonly caused by a carotid artery dissection. Pain from dissection is usually located around the temple and orbit, and may extend from the neck. This condition must be recognized because, in the acute stage, stroke is a possible complication. MRI typically shows an intramural hemorrhage, but in rare cases magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) or cerebral arteriography is needed to provide definitive evidence of dissection.
CST can also cause a Horner syndrome, but patients with this condition are typically ill and often have signs of orbital involvement, such as proptosis, hyperemia, and ophthalmoplegia. A left-sided brain stem stroke would be painless. Temporal arteritis does not cause Horner syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Adie tonic pupil is caused by damage to what structure?
pool.rationale:
Adie tonic pupil is characterized by poor reaction to light, sectoral palsy of the iris sphincter, accommodative paresis, denervation cholinergic supersensitivity, and a strong and tonic pupillary response to near vision (light-near dissociation) followed by slow redilation. It results from damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves carrying postganglionic parasympathetic fibers.
The other choices (trigeminal ganglion, cervical sympathetic ganglion, gasserian ganglion) are incorrect because they do not carry parasympathetic pupillary fibers. The trigeminal (also known as gasserian) ganglion carries synapses for the 3 divisions of cranial nerve V. The cervical sympathetic ganglion carries synapses for sympathetic fibers, damage to these fibers causes anisocoria due to miosis and dilation lag of the involved pupil, as well as ipsilateral ptosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What visual field defect is typical of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy?
pool.rationale: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is a mitochondrial disease. It is more common in males than females. The trait is not transmitted by affected males. Central or cecocentral visual field defects are typical of LHON. Arcuate field defects may be seen with papilledema and glaucoma; altitudinal fields defects commonly are associated with nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy; and bitemporal hemianopia suggests a chiasmal process, such as compression from a pituitary adenoma or craniopharyngioma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient has 2 mm of anisocoria that disappears in bright light. What pharmacologic agent should be used for diagnostic evaluation?
pool.rationale: When encountering anisocoria that is more apparent in dim light, the ophthalmologist should suspect Horner syndrome. Apraclonidine or cocaine drops may be used to assess for appropriate reaction of the affected pupil (dilates with the former, does not react to the latter). Pilocarpine may constrict an abnormally dilated pupil. Tropicamide will dilate most pupils, pathologic or not, while betaxolol has no significant effect on pupillary size.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 48-year-old man has had 3 months of blurred vision OS and has been nicking the left side of his face while shaving. Visual acuity is 20/20 OD, 20/25 OS with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Sensation is reduced over the left forehead and cheek, and the left cornea has an irregular epithelium without lesion or defect. What diagnostic studies are recommended?

options.b: corneal scraping with viral culture and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for herpes simplex virus (HSV)
options.d: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, with gadolinium contrast

pool.rationale:
There is concern that this patient may have a lesion affecting the trigeminal nerve on the left. This is causing reduced sensation of the left side of his face and a neurotrophic cornea, resulting in dryness and blurred vision. The first step in the investigation would be MRI of the brain with gadolinium contrast.
Electromyography and nerve conduction velocity could be part of the workup, but only after the MRI. HSV can cause a neurotrophic cornea, but would not cause numbness of the left side of the face. Urgent orbital exploration and biopsy would only be performed after MRI.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What branch of the posterior cerebral artery supplies the primary visual cortex?
pool.rationale: The distal posterior cerebral artery terminates in the calcarine branch, which supplies the primary visual cortex. The other arteries are branches of the posterior cerebral artery as well but supply different parts of the cortex.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Three weeks ago, a 49-year-old woman developed constant diplopia. She feels well and reports no new headache, fatigue, numbness, or weakness. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU, with equal pupils. Ductions are normal, and at distance there is a 15 PD exotropia in all positions of gaze. Stereopsis is poor even with prism correction. What is the most likely cause of her diplopia?

options.b: sixth-nerve palsy with spread of comitance

pool.rationale:
New-onset diplopia in an adult can result from muscular, neuromuscular, or neurological causes. This patient has full ductions and no constitutional symptoms, such as weakness or headache. Her manifest strabismus is comitant. Comitant misalignment characteristically is found in patients with congenital or early-onset strabismus. Patients with this condition do not typically report diplopia, because there is suppression of the image from one eye. However, they may develop diplopia later in life. For instance, patients with a long-standing exophoria may develop diplopia in their fifth decade of life, when convergence and accommodative capacities decrease.
While there can be a spread of comitance with a sixth-nerve palsy, it does not occur within just a few weeks. She has no other symptoms to suggest increased intracranial pressure. Convergence spasm would not produce constant double vision for 3 weeks and would not produce a comitant misalignment, but it would give a larger-angle strabismus in lateral gazes.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 32-year-old woman has unequal pupils. They measure 4 mm OD and 3 mm OS in the light and 5 mm OD and 4 mm OS in the dark. The pupils react equally to light and dilate equally in the dark. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Anisocoria whose magnitude is equal in dim and bright light indicates that the relative function of the pupillary sphincter and dilator muscles is intact. This scenario is consistent with physiologic anisocoria. Sometimes physiologic anisocoria is more apparent in dim light than in bright light. This can make it difficult to differentiate from a Horner syndrome. In this case, physiologic anisocoria can be differentiated from Horner syndrome through pharmacologic testing.
An Adie pupil and pharmacologic dilation would show anisocoria that is greater in bright light.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with left-sided facial pain, which is present most of the time. She reports that when she is exposed to the cold, windy environment outside she develops electric shock-like jabs affecting the left side of her face. On examination, the ophthalmologist notes hypoesthesia in the cranial nerve V distribution on the left and is concerned for trigeminal neuralgia. What is the most likely cause in this case?

options.a: vascular compression of cranial nerve V

pool.rationale: Trigeminal neuralgia is caused by vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve in 80%-90% of cases. Other potential causes include demyelinating disease, infiltration, and posterior fossa mass. Trigeminal neuralgia also can be primary, with no cause demonstrated; however, the presence of abnormal sensory function on examination makes an underlying lesion more likely.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 50-year-old man presents with a sudden-onset and painless decrease in acuity to 20/70 in the right eye. What test would best distinguish a retinopathy from an optic neuropathy?
pool.rationale:
The photostress recovery test helps to differentiate between retinopathies and optic neuropathies by testing the amount of time it takes for vision to recover after being stimulated with a bright light. The photostress recovery test requires a corrected distance visual acuity of 20/80 or better. The patient is tested monocularly, gazing into a bright light held 2-3 cm from the eye for 10 seconds. Immediately after the light stimulus is removed, the patient attempts to read the next larger Snellen visual acuity line above the previously measured corrected visual acuity (eg, if the patient's corrected visual acuity is 20/25, the 20/30 line would be measured). Normal photostress recovery time is less than 30 seconds, but patients with maculopathy or severe carotid artery stenosis have prolonged recovery times (≥ 90-180 seconds). By contrast, patients with optic neuropathy have normal photostress recovery times.
Both retinopathies and optic neuropathies can cause relative afferent pupillary defects, contrast sensitivity abnormalities, and decreased color vision.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What clinical feature best distinguishes a parietal lobe lesion from an occipital lobe lesion?
pool.rationale: Parietal lobe and occipital lobe lesions can have similar visual field defects (homonymous hemianopia) with normal pupil responses (no relative afferent pupillary defect). Cerebral achromatopsia is a feature of occipital lobe lesions. Pursuit and reflexive saccade movements are initiated in the parietal lobe and as such, abnormal OKN responses can be seen related to a parietal lobe lesion, but not with an occipital lobe lesion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 14-year-old boy complains of intermittent binocular vertical diplopia and eye strain. Examination reveals an intermittent 15 prism diopter right hypertropia that increases in left gaze and right head tilt. Double Maddox rod testing reveals 5 degrees of extorsion of the right eye. What is the most likely etiology?
pool.rationale:
A cranial nerve IV palsy, also known as trochlear nerve palsy, impairs the function of the ipsilateral superior oblique muscle. It causes an ipsilateral hypertropia that is worse on contralateral gaze (adduction) and ipsilateral head tilt, with ipsilateral excyclotorsion. Therefore, a right trochlear nerve palsy would be expected to cause a right hypertropia, worse on left gaze and right head tilt, with right eye excyclotorsion.
A left cranial nerve IV palsy would be expected to demonstrate a left hypertropia, worse on right gaze and left head tilt. It would be associated with left excyclotorsion on double Maddox rod testing.
Brown syndrome is a restrictive form of strabismus producing an ipsilateral hypotropia on adduction with improvement in abduction. Forced duction testing would show restricted elevation in adduction, accentuated with retropulsion to stretch the superior oblique tendon.
A skew deviation would have a pattern different from cranial nerve palsies, such as a right hypertropia with ipsilateral incyclotorsion. Lesion origin is in the brainstem or vestibular apparatus and often has other neurologic signs.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An asymptomatic, otherwise healthy 38-year-old patient has small, irregular pupils that react minimally to light stimulus. With attempted reading, the pupils become even smaller. What investigation, if any, should be performed to identify the cause of this condition?

options.b: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of orbits with contrast

pool.rationale:
The patient is demonstrating light-near dissociation with brisk near pupillary response in the absence of a good light response. The small, irregular pupils in this context raise the possibility of Argyll Robertson pupils, which are associated with advanced syphilitic infection. Similar findings can be found in widespread autonomic neuropathies, including diabetes and chronic alcoholism. In this case, testing for syphilis should be performed. If the test result is positive, referral to an infectious disease specialist for further evaluation and treatment should be made.
Orbital lesions are extremely unlikely to cause bilateral pupil findings of this sort. Apraclonidine testing is used for diagnosis of Horner syndrome and is not indicated in this case. Observation is inappropriate, since there is concern for syphilis in this case.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with optic nerve drusen should be informed about what potential complication of this condition?
pool.rationale:
Optic nerve head drusen are refractile, often calcified nodules located within the optic nerve head. They are associated with stationary or progressive visual field defects. Visual fields should be monitored over time.
Although the segmental area of damage may become atrophic, generalized optic atrophy with subsequent central visual loss and reduced color vision is unlikely. Serous retinal detachments would not be expected.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 27-year-old woman notes that her right pupil has been larger than the left since yesterday. Vision is 20/20 OU at distance, J10 OD and J1+ OS at near. Her right pupil is 8 mm and does not react to direct, consensual, or near stimulus. There is no segmental constriction of the iris. Motility is normal and there is no ptosis. What occupation puts the patient at higher risk for this problem?
pool.rationale:
This patient has a dilated pupil and difficulty with accommodation in that eye. There is no segmental constriction of the iris to suggest an Adie pupil. There is no ptosis or ophthalmoplegia to suggest a third nerve palsy. These findings are most consistent with pharmacologic dilation.
Intensive care nurses often have to handle scopolamine patches or atropine, which if inadvertently exposed to the eye will cause pharmacologic dilation of the pupil.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What functional action of the superior oblique muscle contributes to the exotropia seen in a complete third nerve palsy?
pool.rationale: In a complete third nerve palsy, the only functioning EOMs are the lateral rectus and superior oblique. The tertiary action of the superior oblique is abduction that exacerbates the outward position (exotropia) of the eye.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 20-year-old man suffered head trauma during a motor vehicle accident and has noted pulsatile synchronous tinnitus and horizontal diplopia since the accident. Examination revealed enlarged, corkscrew, arterialized conjunctival blood vessels of the left eye. He was also noted to have a left sixth nerve palsy and an audible bruit over the left eye. On neuroimaging, what vessel would be expected to be dilated in this patient?
pool.rationale:
This patient has classic signs and symptoms of a direct carotid-cavernous sinus fistula. High-flow, direct fistulas most commonly occur after severe head trauma and produce a cranial bruit. Carotid-cavernous sinus fistulas often produce elevated intraocular pressure, proptosis, and arterialization of conjunctival vessels. Compression of cranial nerve VI (CN VI) by an enlarged inferior petrosal sinus that drains the fistula can cause a sixth nerve palsy.
Abnormal connections between the carotid artery or its branches and the cavernous sinus introduce high arterial pressures into the normally low-pressure venous circulation of the cavernous sinus. Such a high-pressure connection may reverse blood flow within the superior ophthalmic vein, leading to an enlarged and dilated superior ophthalmic vein.
The other vessels listed (vein of Galen, superior sagittal sinus, ophthalmic artery) would not be expected to be enlarged from a carotid-cavernous sinus fistula.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When describing perceptual derangements in a patient following demyelinating optic neuritis, what is the term for the illusion of an object that moves in an elliptical path rather than a straight line?
pool.rationale: Due to the relative conduction delay within an optic nerve that has been affected by demyelinating optic neuritis compared with the contralateral unaffected optic nerve, an object moving in a single plane might be perceived as tracing an elliptical rather than straight path. This illusion is called the Pulfrich phenomenon. Riddoch phenomenon refers to the ability to see moving, but not static, objects in a blind hemifield (staticokinetic dissociation). Palinopsia is the preservation of a visual image after removal of the original stimulus. Optic ataxia is the inability to perform visually guided movements.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A pupil-involving complete third cranial nerve palsy presenting in a patient with simultaneous onset of contralateral weakness localizes to what brainstem structure?

options.a: ipsilateral midbrain third nerve fascicle in the territory of the cerebral peduncle
options.b: ipsilateral midbrain third nerve fascicle in the territory of the red nucleus
options.d: ipsilateral midbrain third nerve fascicle in the territory of the cerebellar peduncle

pool.rationale:
Fascicular ocular motor cranial nerve palsies are caused by lesions of the nerve distal to the nerve's nucleus but within the confines of the brainstem. Involvement of the third nerve fascicle can produce 1 of 4 different syndromes:
  1. Weber syndrome = third nerve palsy + contralateral hemiparesis. This occurs due to damage to the ventral midbrain in the territory of the cerebral peduncle.
  2. Benedikt syndrome = third nerve palsy + contralateral ataxia/tremor. This occurs due to damage to the red nucleus and substantia nigra.
  3. Claude syndrome = third nerve palsy + contralateral ataxia. This occurs due to damage to the dorsal midbrain, involving the superior cerebellar peduncle.
  4. Nothnagel syndrome = nuclear third nerve lesion with features of supranuclear eye movement dysfunction + ataxia. This occurs due to damage in the dorsal midbrain.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with binocular vertical diplopia after noncontact whiplash injury from a motor vehicle accident. What would be the most useful clinical test to determine the etiology of the diplopia?
pool.rationale:
A patient complaining of diplopia after noncontact trauma most likely has injury to one of the 3 motor cranial nerves (CN) supplying the extraocular muscles (III, IV, VI). Binocular vertical diplopia suggests that there is strabismus involving the vertical extraocular muscles (eliminating CN VI injury as a possibility), rather than monocular diplopia (which could be tested with pinhole).
Of the 3 motor cranial nerves, the oculomotor is the most robust and has the most direct route from the brainstem to the orbit. It is therefore least likely to be injured in a noncontact trauma. Traumatic CN III paresis or palsy typically requires severe head trauma and is usually associated with basal skull fractures and intracranial bleeding.
In contrast, the IV and VI nerve follow circuitous routes from the brainstem into the orbit and are therefore quite vulnerable to injury, even after seemingly trivial head trauma. Furthermore, the trochlear nerve is the smallest cranial nerve, containing a mere 1500 axons.
The Bielschowsky head tilt test is used as part of the "3-step test" to diagnose a CN IV palsy. In CN IV palsy, the mantra for diagnosis is a vertical deviation that manifests "a hypertropia on the same side that gets worse on opposite gaze and same head tilt."
In noncontact trauma, forced ductions would be expected to be negative, as there would not be any reason for muscle entrapment or scarring. While CN IV palsies may have torsional effects that can be measured with double Maddox rod testing, the Bielschowsky 3-step test is more helpful in the diagnosis of acute vertical diplopia from CN IV palsy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with unilateral upper eyelid retraction on ipsilateral attempted adduction. What is the most likely cause of this finding?

options.b: aberrant regeneration of cranial nerve (CN) III

pool.rationale:
Cranial nerve III palsies displaying aberrant regeneration have a variety of clinical presentations, one of which is upper eyelid retraction on attempted adduction. Other common findings are pupillary miosis with attempted eyelid elevation, adduction, or infraduction. These findings are caused by nerve axon damage, such as compression from a slowly expanding mass in the cavernous sinus, leading to nerve fiber misrouting that produces several synkinetic phenomena (ie, co-contraction of muscles that normally are not activated together).
Thyroid eye disease is the most common cause of upper eyelid retraction but is not triggered by adduction. Dorsal midbrain syndrome is a bilateral condition where upper eyelid retraction (Collier sign) occurs due to compression of the posterior midbrain, but it manifests with convergence insufficiency and impaired upgaze, and is not triggered by adduction. Lastly, Duane syndrome produces a narrowed, not widened, interpalpebral fissure on adduction, due to anomalous co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscles of the involved eye or eyes, which causes globe retraction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What imaging technique may be contraindicated in some patients with cochlear implants?
pool.rationale:
Cochlear implants historically are contraindicated in MRI because the majority of implants have a magnet that can interact with the MRI. However, it should be noted that there are safe ways of obtaining MRI in many patients with cochlear implants (taking into account whether the magnetic component of the cochlear implant is removable, as well as the Tesla strength of the MRI being used). In the clinical setting, the specific manufacturer recommendations for the patient's device must be examined on an individual basis.
Table 2-1 in the American Academy of Ophthalmology's publication, Basic and Clinical Science Course, Section 5. Neuro-Ophthalmology, lists the advantages, disadvantages, and contraindications to various imaging modalities.


(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 62-year-old man with Parkinson disease is having difficulty opening his eyes. The examination shows no eyelid spasms, and he often stimulates eyelid opening by pressing on his brows. He has no ptosis once the eyelids are open. What ocular condition does he have?
pool.rationale: This patient has apraxia of eyelid opening, which can occur in isolation but also as part of Parkinson disease. Patients with this motor abnormality appear to be unable to generate a voluntary stimulus to activate the levator subnucleus in the midbrain, and they may use tactile stimuli to the face to overcome this problem. Levator muscle function is normal, and patients do not develop ptosis from the condition. Botulinum toxin injection to the pretarsal orbicularis oculi may be effective, although the mechanism is not entirely clear.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 18-month-old infant presents with mild upper eyelid ptosis, lower eyelid elevation, and an ipsilateral miotic but reactive pupil with iris heterochromia. This child should be evaluated for what possible tumor?
pool.rationale: This child's clinical features are characteristic of Horner syndrome. A child with acquired Horner syndrome (ie, without a history of birth trauma) should be screened for neuroblastoma, which often presents as an acquired Horner syndrome. Neuroblastoma is one of the most common childhood cancers and usually originates in either the adrenal gland or the sympathetic ganglion chain in the retroperitoneum or mediastinum, a location that leads to interruption of papillary sympathetic innervation or Horner syndrome. Neuroblastoma is the most frequent source of childhood orbital metastasis. Retinoblastoma most commonly presents as leukocoria, while other signs may include strabismus, hemorrhage, hyphema, ocular or periocular inflammation, glaucoma, proptosis, or hypopyon. Rhabdomyosarcoma commonly presents with proptosis, ptosis, or strabismus. Wilms tumor originates in the kidney and rarely metastasizes to the orbit.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What magnetic resonance imaging  (MRI) sequence is best for detecting periventricular white matter changes in multiple sclerosis?
pool.rationale:
FLAIR imaging provides T2-weighted images without the bright cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) signal, which can obscure adjacent pathology. Therefore, FLAIR is ideal for detecting periventricular white matter lesions.
DWI is ideal for identifying recent infarctions. T1-weighted images are optimal for demonstrating anatomy. STIR provides T1-weighted images without the confounding bright fat signal and can be useful for orbital and spinal cord evaluation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the primary reason that patients with demyelinating optic neuritis should not be treated with oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day alone?

options.a: Oral steroid does not promote visual recovery.
options.b: Steroid side-effects are greater than with IV treatment.
options.c: Treated patients have a higher multiple sclerosis (MS) risk.
options.d: This treatment increases risk of recurrence.

pool.rationale:
Patients in the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) were randomized to treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone (250 mg IV q6hr for 3 days) followed by 1 mg/kg/day prednisone for 11 days then a quick taper, oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day only for 14 days, or placebo. Patients in all groups had excellent visual recovery with no difference in visual outcome at 6 months.
Steroid side effects between the 2 treated groups were similar. Steroid treatment (regardless of route) reduced the risk of MS in the first 2 years after treatment, but not thereafter. However, patients treated only with oral prednisone had a higher rate of optic neuritis recurrence than both the high-dose IV and placebo-treated patients. Therefore, oral prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day is not recommended as a treatment for optic neuritis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 73-year-old woman developed frequent episodic left-sided spasms involving her orbicularis oculi and facial muscles, lasting a few seconds to minutes at a time. What is the most common cause of her symptoms?
pool.rationale:
The patient's symptoms are consistent with hemifacial spasm. The pathogenesis of hemifacial spasm is most commonly compression of the seventh nerve root exit zone by an aberrant vessel. Less commonly, tumors within the cerebellopontine angle or previous injury to cranial nerve (CN) VII may lead to the spasms; therefore, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is typically performed to exclude a compressive lesion.
Neurodegenerative conditions, such as Parkinson disease, and basal ganglion infarction can be associated with blepharospasm, not hemifacial spasm.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 75-year-old woman presents for a routine examination. In bright light her pupils measure 3.5 mm OD and 3 mm OS, and in dim light they measure 5 mm OD and 4.5 mm OS. She has 1 mm ptosis OD, normal levator function, and normal ocular motility. What is the most appropriate next step?
pool.rationale: This patient has physiologic anisocoria with the same pupil disparity between bright and dim lighting conditions. Despite mild ptosis, the normal motility and levator function strongly suggest that the anisocoria is not due to a CN III palsy. Even if the ptosis were on the side of the smaller left pupil, the findings are not consistent with Horner syndrome (anisocoria should be worse in dim light). Absent evidence for an urgent process, imaging and/or hospitalization are not indicated at this time.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents for evaluation of diplopia. With a simple occluder in front of the right eye, the diplopia goes away; with the occluder in front of the left eye, the diplopia persists. With the left eye occluded, placing a pinhole occluder over the right eye resolves the diplopia. The manifest refraction is plano sphere in each eye. Corneal topography is normal. Ductions and versions are full. Nuclear cataracts with vacuoles are noted in each eye. There is intermediate dry macular degeneration present in the right eye and early dry macular degeneration in the left eye. The optic nerves are normal. What is the most likely cause of this patient's double vision?
pool.rationale: Inhomogeneous cataracts frequently split the incident light into 2 or more divergent paths, resulting in monocular diplopia. Dry age-related macular degeneration may reduce retinal sensitivity to the diminished retinal illumination seen through a pinhole, but it does not cause double vision. (Macular edema may cause monocular diplopia, however.) Recently acquired strabismus frequently causes binocular diplopia, but this resolves if either eye is covered. This patient does not have any astigmatism, as evidenced by no refractive error and normal corneal topography.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 58-year-old man was recently diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. He also has a past medical history of hypertension, gout, and stroke. His medications include allopurinol, furosemide, prednisone, and warfarin. Which of those medications may be causing or worsening the myasthenia gravis?
pool.rationale: Myasthenia gravis (MG) can be caused, unmasked, or worsened by antiarrhythmics, statins, antibiotics, chemotherapeutic drugs, antiepileptic drugs, quinolones, penicillamine, corticosteroids, beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers. Allopurinol has not been shown to worsen symptoms of myasthenia gravis. Furosemide is a diuretic, and warfarin is a blood thinner.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What clinical test best localizes monocular diplopia to an optical etiology?
pool.rationale: Monocular diplopia most commonly results from abnormalities in the refractive media, though less commonly retinal pathology and cerebral monocular diplopia (very rare) may cause monocular diplopia. Monocular diplopia that resolves with pinhole establishes that the diplopia is a result of an optical aberration and obviates the need for a neurological workup. Though corneal topography and optical coherence tomography may help evaluate monocular causes of monocular diplopia, they do not prove an optical etiology. A manifest refraction may help resolve many forms of monocular diplopia but is not always successful (irregular astigmatism, dry eyes, cataracts are just some examples in which a manifest refraction may not completely resolve monocular diplopia from an optical cause).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Chronic, progressive visual field loss with persistent headaches in a patient with pseudotumor cerebri despite weight loss and maximal oral medical therapy is an indication for what treatment?
pool.rationale:
In a patient unresponsive to medical therapy, surgical intervention is warranted. If headaches are a significant component, a ventriculoperitoneal shunt is probably the most appropriate procedure. If a patient were to have progressive vision loss without headaches, an optic nerve sheath fenestration would be most appropriate. However, sometimes the most appropriate procedure is the one that is the most easily available for the patient.
Orbital decompression is not used for pseudotumor cerebri. Intravenous prednisone is used for optic neuritis. Intravenous mannitol is used to lower intraocular pressure.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with involuntary, large amplitude, multidirectional eye movements. What underlying neoplasm is most concerning in this patient?
pool.rationale: This patient has opsoclonus, which sometimes can occur along with myoclonus and ataxia. Etiologies include paraneoplastic syndromes, encephalitis, drug intoxication, multiple sclerosis, environmental toxins, and hyperosmolar coma. Workup includes searching for an underlying tumor and associated paraneoplastic syndrome. In children, neuroblastoma is the primary consideration. In adults, small-cell lung carcinoma, breast cancer, and ovarian cancer are of the most concern.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 55-year-old woman was recently started on a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) and then developed severe recurrent headaches with hemianopic field loss. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) showed a “string-of-beads” appearance of the cerebral arteries. What is her most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) is characterized by severe recurrent headaches with or without focal neurologic deficits and/or seizures, as well as segmental constriction of cerebral arteries that resolves within 3 months. Visual complaints are frequent and include light sensitivity, blurred vision, and hemianopic visual field loss. This syndrome mainly affects middle-aged women, and more than one-half of RCVS cases occur during the postpartum period or after exposure to vasoactive substances (eg, SSRIs). MRA may demonstrate the characteristic “string-of-beads” appearance of the cerebral arteries.
Cerebral vasculitis and cerebral arterial dissection can cause similar symptoms, but would not typically show the classic “string-of-beads” appearance of segmental constriction of the arteries that is seen in RCVS. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome causes T2 signal abnormalities and is not typically associated with severe headaches.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 34-year-old woman with a metallic foreign body has head and neck pain and notes new left upper eyelid ptosis. Her right pupil is larger than the left and redilates more briskly after direct or consensual stimulus. What is the most appropriate imaging test to obtain first?

options.b: computed tomography (CT) angiogram of the brain
options.c: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain

pool.rationale: The patient has signs and symptoms to suggest a painful left-sided Horner syndrome with recent onset. Cervical carotid dissection must be excluded, and either CT or MR angiography of the neck should be performed as the initial test. Brain/head studies are not adequate to evaluate the area of concern. Catheter angiography may be done if the CTA or MRA is abnormal but is not the first test to be ordered. In fact, it may be less sensitive for initial diagnosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A hypertensive adult experienced onset of complete left ptosis 2 days ago. There is anisocoria and partial limitation of ductions in the left eye. What is the most appropriate initial management strategy?

options.a: referral to primary care physician for more aggressive control of hypertension
options.b: observation as long as there is no diplopia
options.c: imaging to rule out intracranial aneurysm
options.d: Tensilon test to rule out myasthenia gravis (MG)

pool.rationale: The description is of a patient with pupil-involving third nerve palsy, and the usual causes are intracranial aneurysm, microvascular infarction, and diabetes. An aneurysm may be fatal and must be ruled out. Observation is not appropriate. A Tensilon test may be indicated if the initial workup is negative, and if there is variability of ptosis and strabismus on examination. Hypertension should be controlled, but an aneurysm needs to be ruled out first.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 50-year-old man complains of painless binocular vertical diplopia. He presents with a left head tilt and has an 8 prism-diopter (PD) right hypertropia in primary position. This hypertropia measures 12 PD in left gaze and 3 PD in right gaze. On right head tilt his hypertropia measures 13 PD and on left tilt it is 2 PD. What would suggest a congenital right fourth nerve palsy in this patient?

options.a: old photos that show the absence of a head tilt
options.b: left hypertropia of 8 PD on downgaze and right hypertropia of 12 PD on upgaze
options.c: the patient's denial of diplopia in primary position
options.d: no hypertropia when the patient looks up and to the right

pool.rationale:
If the patient denies diplopia in primary position; this indicates that he has a vertical fusional amplitude of at least 8 prism diopters (normal is 1-3 PD). Patients with a long-standing fourth nerve palsy have a relatively large vertical fusional range (>3 prism diopters). Most patients maintain a chronic head tilt. The long-standing nature of the head tilt may cause facial asymmetry and can often be confirmed by reviewing old photographs.
A right fourth nerve palsy will increase in left gaze and right head tilt. Hypertropia when the patient is looking up and to the right would be expected to be less in any right fourth nerve palsy, and therefore does not help distinguish a congenital fourth nerve palsy from other causes of a fourth nerve palsy. A left hypertropia on downgaze and right hypertropia on upgaze would not be expected in a right fourth nerve palsy of any etiology.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What additional physical finding would be expected for an infarct involving the fascicle of the sixth nerve?
pool.rationale:
The seventh nerve loops around the sixth nerve nucleus within the pons. Therefore, a lesion affecting the fascicle of the sixth nerve can affect the ipsilateral seventh nerve, causing ipsilateral facial paralysis. The fascicle of the sixth nerve extends ventrally and passes adjacent to the corticospinal tract before leaving the ventral pons.
Involvement of the corticospinal tract will cause contralateral weakness (Raymond syndrome), not ipsilateral weakness. Convergence-retraction nystagmus is seen in dorsal midbrain syndrome, which would not cause an abduction deficit. Contralateral homonymous hemianopia indicates a postchiasmal lesion within the visual pathway, which would not be caused by a lesion involving the fascicle of the sixth nerve.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 41-year-old woman develops sudden vision loss in her right eye. Visual acuity is 20/50 in the right eye associated with a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) and an inferior visual field defect on confrontation. Visual acuity and confrontation field in the left eye is normal. Optic discs and fundi appear normal in both eyes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.a: compressive optic neuropathy from a meningioma

pool.rationale:
Patients with optic neuritis and compressive optic neuropathy can have normal appearing optic nerves despite vision loss. According to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT), the optic disc appears normal in 65% of cases of optic neuritis. In this patient, however, the acute onset argues for optic neuritis because compressive etiologies, especially from a slow-growing meningioma, typically present with slowly progressive vision loss.
Acute vision loss in the presence of a normal optic nerve and macula is unlikely to be anterior ischemic optic neuropathy or branch retinal vein occlusion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with normal visual fields undergoes pattern-reversal visual evoked potential (VEP) testing. In one eye, the P100 wave has a preserved amplitude, but it is markedly prolonged. The other eye has a normal amplitude and latency. What condition should be suspected?
pool.rationale:
Visual evoked potential (VEP) testing measures electrical signals produced in response to a visual stimulus; the signals are recorded at the scalp overlying the occipital cortex. Damage anywhere along the afferent visual pathway can reduce the amplitude or speed of the signal. Because the central visual field predominates in the occipital cortex, isolated peripheral vision loss may yield normal VEP results. A common cause of delayed latency on VEP with normal visual fields is a prior bout of recovered demyelinating optic neuritis. Multiple sclerosis is the most common cause of optic neuritis. Demyelination of the optic nerve results in increased latency of the P100 waveform without significant effect on amplitude, whereas ischemic, compressive, and toxic damage reduce amplitude primarily, with less effect on latency.
Glaucoma would not cause a delayed VEP unless there was significant visual field loss. Cortical blindness can cause delayed VEP, but it would affect both eyes.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A person presents with ptosis and horizontal gaze palsy associated with ataxia and areflexia. What is the diagnosis?

options.a: Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome
options.c: cerebrovascular infarction of the abducens nucleus

pool.rationale:
Areflexia, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia characterize Miller Fisher syndrome, a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Any pattern of ophthalmoplegia can be seen in Miller Fisher syndrome. Patients can also have bilateral ptosis, facial diplegia, and respiratory and swallowing difficulties.
Myasthenia gravis, giant cell arteritis, or an infarction to the abducens nucleus can cause horizontal gaze palsy but would not cause ataxia or areflexia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 56-year-old woman presents for evaluation of right eye irritation. She additionally reports a 3-day history of altered taste sensation and right-sided facial weakness, and is noted to have dense interpalpebral keratopathy, incomplete blink, and orbicularis oculi weakness on the right. Five (5) days later she presents with similar findings affecting the left side. Infection with what organism is most likely the cause of these findings?
pool.rationale:
Borrelia burgdorferi

The patient in this case presents with bilateral sequential facial nerve palsy. The tick-borne spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative organism of Lyme disease, and can be associated with unilateral or bilateral facial nerve palsy. As many as 25% of cases of new-onset facial nerve palsies may be attributed to B burgdorferi infection in endemic areas.
Actinomyces israelii is associated with canaliculitis. Staphylococcus aureus causes staphylococcal infection, and Bartonella henselae causes cat-scratch disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 57-year-old man developed severe left orbital pain, decreased vision in the left eye, and a vesicular rash involving the left upper face and eyelid. On examination, he had ophthalmoplegia. Visual acuity was 20/400 OS and there was a left afferent pupillary defect (APD). Dilated fundus examination showed mild optic disc swelling without hemorrhages in the left eye, normal in the right. Where does this constellation of findings localize?
pool.rationale: The presence of a vesicular rash involving the V1 distribution is highly suggestive of herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Zoster can affect any part of the eye and can rarely cause an orbital apex syndrome. This patient has ophthalmoplegia and an optic neuropathy, which localizes to the orbital apex. Cavernous sinus involvement would lead to ophthalmoplegia without optic neuropathy. An optic chiasm lesion would cause a bitemporal hemianopia. Scleritis would cause pain without vision loss or ophthalmoplegia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with continuous unilateral undulating contraction of the orbicularis oculi and most of the facial muscles. What is the most common cause of these symptoms?

options.d: aberrant regeneration resulting from prior Bell palsy

pool.rationale: Facial myokymia is usually the result of a pontine glioma or demyelination (ie, MS). It is characterized by continuous unilateral contraction of facial muscle bundles and typically signifies intramedullary disease of the pons involving the CN VII nucleus or fascicle. Compression of the CN VII root exit zone by an aberrant vessel is the most common cause of hemifacial spasm, which is characterized by a unilateral episodic spasm involving the facial musculature. Excessive caffeine intake can cause isolated eyelid myokymia. Aberrant regeneration after facial palsy is typically not continuous.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 7-month-old infant develops conjugate horizontal nystagmus with a null point. The infant maintains attention on a fixation target and follows it well, aside from the noted nystagmus. Testing with an optokinetic drum shows a reversal of the normally expected optokinetic nystagmus. The eye examination is normal and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is normal. What is the most likely underlying etiology?
pool.rationale:
Infantile nystagmus syndrome (INS), also called congenital nystagmus, is classically described as a binocular conjugate horizontal nystagmus that presents within the first 2 years of life. It is categorized as either congenital motor nystagmus (CMN) or congenital sensory nystagmus, depending on the etiology. Congenital motor nystagmus (CMN) is not associated with afferent pathway disease, is often associated with normal or near-normal vision, has a normal ocular examination and normal neuroimaging, and does not produce oscillopsia. In contrast, sensory nystagmus arises when central visual acuity is too poor to develop a stable fixational mechanism. Sensory nystagmus is associated with conditions that cause bilateral, pregeniculate vision loss in children younger than 2 years. Because congenital motor and congenital sensory nystagmus can present and appear identical, workup of a patient with early-onset nystagmus should include a search for clinical manifestations of pregeniculate vision loss. In the absence of obvious ocular causes such as cataract, the patient should be evaluated for the following conditions, which can be subtle and difficult to detect in uncooperative children: optic neuropathy, foveal hypoplasia, and retinal dystrophy.
Approximately two-thirds of CMN patients exhibit a paradoxical inversion of the optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) response, which is unique to CMN. Normally, when a patient with right-jerk nystagmus views an optokinetic drum rotation to the patient's left (eliciting a "pursuit left, jerk right" response), the intensity of the right-jerk nystagmus increases. However, patients with CMN exhibit a damped right-jerk nystagmus or possibly even a left-jerk nystagmus when viewing an optokinetic drum rotation to the left.
X-linked mutations in the FERM domain-containing-7 gene (FRMD7) underlie many cases of typical CMN. Intracranial brain tumors do not cause CMN. Poor fusion in a child causes fusion maldevelopment nystagmus. Chiasmal/suprachiasmal tumors such as optic pathway gliomas can result in a nystagmus identical to spasmus nutans.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What type of nystagmus is characterized by reversal of the normal pattern of optokinetic nystagmus?
pool.rationale:
Congenital nystagmus, or infantile nystagmus syndrome, is often recognized in the first few months of life. It is usually conjugate and horizontal in all positions of gaze.
There are 2 characteristic signs of congenital nystagmus:
  1. Reversal of the normal pattern of optokinetic nystagmus (OKN), characterized by slow-phase eye movements in the direction opposite that of the rotating OKN drum.
  2. Pattern in which the velocity of slow-phase movement increases exponentially with distance from fixation. Identification of this pattern requires eye movement recordings.
Latent nystagmus is an early-onset, conjugate, horizontal jerk nystagmus that is accentuated when one eye is occluded.
Spasmus nutans is a childhood nystagmus characterized by asymmetric, small-amplitude, high-frequency, shimmering eye movements. It often is associated with head nodding and torticollis.
Gaze-evoked nystagmus develops due to inability to maintain fixation in eccentric gaze, leading to the eyes drifting back to the midline. A corrective saccade is then generated to reposition the eyes on the eccentric target, meaning that the fast phase is always in the direction of gaze.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 66-year-old woman has repeated transient vision loss in her right eye lasting for 10-15 minutes. She is otherwise well. Her ophthalmic examination is normal, as are erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C‑reactive protein results. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain shows a focus of diffusion-weighted imaging abnormality in the right parietal area. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.a: intravenous corticosteroids and temporal artery biopsy
options.b: immediate evaluation in a hospital stroke unit

pool.rationale:
Transient monocular vision loss (TMVL) may herald cerebrovascular disease, usually of the ipsilateral internal carotid artery, that can place the patient at risk for hemispheric stroke. Data from the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial (NASCET) suggested that TMVL was less likely to result in stroke than other types of transient ischemic attacks (TIA). More recent data suggest that patients with TMVL should be evaluated with urgent brain MRI to look for diffuse-weighted imaging (DWI) abnormalities, as their presence indicates that cerebral ischemia has occurred recently. Such patients may be at high risk for stroke, and they may benefit from rapid surgical treatment of vascular disease. Having such patients seen in a hospital stroke unit is the most effective way to ensure they receive immediate evaluation.
Giant cell arteritis must be considered as a cause of TMVL as well, but in this patient, the normal ESR and CRP, along with absence of symptoms, as well as the DWI abnormality, indicates that she needs stroke evaluation. Scheduling routine carotid ultrasonography or simply prescribing aspirin is not adequate.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What diagnostic test is most helpful in the workup of a 12-year-old boy with right-sided proptosis and chronic unilateral optic disc edema?
pool.rationale:
While IVFA and OCT can help characterize the presence and severity of optic disc edema, proptosis with chronic optic disc edema suggests an orbital mass, which is proven only with imaging behind the globe. Magnetic resonance imaging, especially with intravenous gadolinium contrast and fat-suppressed views of the orbits, offers coronal and axial soft tissue views of the optic nerve and its sheath. This imaging modality shows intrinsic and extrinsic lesions of the optic nerve with high resolution. Optic nerve biopsy is too invasive as a first diagnostic test and is often unnecessary to diagnose the characteristic fusiform lesion morphology of optic nerve glioma, which is the most common optic nerve tumor of this age group.
(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: A 36-year-old male presents with binocular horizontal diplopia following a severe head injury with left medial orbital trauma. He is noted to have 20 prism diopters of esotropia in primary gaze, worse in left gaze, improving in right gaze. He has a large left abduction deficit. He has left upper and lower eyelid edema and ecchymosis. There is no enophthalmos or proptosis. His eye examination is otherwise unremarkable. What test is most appropriate for determining whether his ocular motility deficit is a result of a paretic or restrictive etiology?
pool.rationale:
This patient has an incomitant esotropia following trauma. Given the pattern of esotropia (worse in left gaze, improved in right gaze) and the left abduction deficit, this could represent either a paresis of the left lateral rectus muscle (left CN6 palsy from a closed head injury) or a restriction of the left medial rectus (which can occur with left medial orbital trauma).
Saccadic velocities are a simple method for helping to distinguish between a paretic and restrictive etiology. Paretic etiologies typically result in decreased saccadic velocities, whereas restrictive etiologies typically have a normal saccadic velocity. However, in cases where the saccadic velocity may not be easily ascertained (for example, a near-ophthalmoplegic eye), forced duction testing may be useful. A doll's eye test is useful in differentiating between supranuclear and nuclear/infranuclear causes of limited eye motility. A double Maddox rod test is used to quantify torsional strabismus.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 88-year-old female presents for evaluation of diplopia following a brainstem stroke. What clinical finding would suggest a nuclear right cranial nerve (CN) III palsy?
pool.rationale: The CN III nuclear complex consists of paired subnuclei for the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique muscles, as well as paired subnuclei for the pupillary constrictor muscles and a single subnucleus for the levator palpebrae muscles. The subnuclei for the superior rectus supply the contralateral superior rectus muscle; as such, a right nuclear CN III may have a left superior rectus palsy. A nuclear CN III lesion could either spare or affect both eyelids; a unilateral ptosis in the setting of a CN III palsy would suggest an infranuclear lesion. A right nuclear CN III lesion would cause right pupil dilation, not left pupil dilation. A right medial rectus palsy may be present but is not specific to a nuclear CN III palsy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Neuro-Ophthalmology — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 37-year-old man reports poor peripheral vision in both eyes for 6 months, and perimetry shows severe field constriction to less than 10 degrees in both eyes. He makes accurate saccades in all directions. Tangent screen testing at 1 meter shows a larger field than at 2 meters. Pupils are briskly reactive. What is the most likely finding on fundus examination?
pool.rationale: This patient has nonphysiological visual field loss (ie, it is not consistent with neurologic or ophthalmic disease), as demonstrated by his smaller tangent screen field at 2 meters vs 1 meter. Patients with severe visual field constriction from organic disease should have visual field expansion, as they are positioned farther away from the tangent screen. Thus, his fundus examination should be normal.

pool.q: What systemic disease is commonly associated with myasthenia gravis (MG)?

options.d: granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly termed Wegener granulomatosis)

pool.rationale: Because there is a high coexistence of MG with other autoimmune disorders, serologic testing should be done for thyroid dysfunction and systemic lupus erythematosus.

pool.q: What supranuclear structure, if damaged, can be associated with diplopia and strabismus?
pool.rationale:
Most supranuclear disorders affect both eyes equally and therefore do not cause diplopia. However, certain supranuclear lesions do not result in a symmetric effect and thus may produce ocular misalignment and diplopia.

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)
